blocks.h: A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
Everyone has a room they do not go into.

Not a metaphor, and not a trauma in the clinical sense. Just a room. A thought you had once and were frightened by. Something you wanted and should not have wanted. A moment you were present at and have never described accurately to anybody, including yourself, including in the dark, including now.

Most people manage this extremely well. That is the thing nobody says out loud. The doors hold. People go to work and raise children and are decent to strangers with the room still in the house, and they are not lying and they are not ill, and there is nothing underneath waiting to be released.
This imprint has spent sixty-one books saying: bring your ugliest thought, there is a chair for it. Sit down. Say it out loud. Nothing you have in you is beyond being written down and looked at.
I would like to enter one qualification, and this is the book where I do it.
That is not true in every case.

Some doors are load-bearing. Some people are standing up because of what they are not looking at, and the strength is real, and the life built on it is real, and the kindness is real, and opening the door does not make any of it more real. It only means a man is on a floor.
I have watched people be opened by professionals who meant it kindly. I have watched a few of them not get up.

The man in this book is the strongest person I have written. He is generous and self-made and awake, and he has done more with less than almost anybody I know. And every single one of those qualities is also the hand on the door.
I am not telling you to keep it shut. I am telling you that I do not know, and that anybody who is certain either way is selling something.
Bring your ugliest thought. There is a chair for it.
But look at the door on your way past, and be honest with yourself about what it is holding up.
Chew Z
PART ONE — THE FLOOR
1. THE YEARS — 2010
Nobody met me.

I want to start there because for eleven years I have listened to people describe their own arrivals and there is always somebody at the barrier. A cousin with a sign. An uncle who has taken the afternoon off. A woman crying into a phone.

I came out of customs at Tom Bradley at twenty past two in the afternoon on the eighteenth of May 2010, with one suitcase and a canvas bag, and the doors opened and there was a crowd of about three hundred people and not one of them was for me.

My cousin Farhad was going to come and then his shift changed. He texted. It was a completely reasonable text. He gave me the address and told me to take a shuttle and said he’d leave the key with the manager, and all of that worked exactly as described.
I stood there for about four minutes anyway.

Not upset. Not lost. Just standing in the airport in a country I had never been in, with a bag, watching other people’s families do the thing families do at barriers, and thinking — and I remember this precisely, it is one of maybe six thoughts I can date to the minute — thinking:
All right. So it’s this.
And then I went and found the shuttle.
I was twenty-one years old and I had two hands that did not fully close and about nine hundred dollars.

Farhad’s apartment was in Van Nuys, on a street with four palm trees on it, and the palm trees were the first thing that got me. Not because they were beautiful. Because they were exactly the same as the ones in the films, and that is a very stupid thing to be moved by, and I sat down on the step of that building with my suitcase and looked at a palm tree for a while like a tourist.
The heat was the second thing. It was May and it was dry and the air smelled of hot dust and somebody’s laundry and gasoline, and it was, and I did not know how to say this at the time, familiar. Los

Angeles in May smells more like Tehran in Mordad [mor-DAAD] than anywhere else on earth. Two enormous dry cities in a bowl with mountains behind them and too many cars. I have met people who found California alien. I was not one of them. I got off a shuttle in the San Fernando Valley and my body said: yes, this. I know this shape.
The floor was a foam mattress in the front room and I slept on it for six weeks.
I called my mother that night. It was morning there.
My mother’s name is Layla [LEY-laa]. I have not written it down in eleven years except on forms, and it looks strange to me on a page, the way your own handwriting does in somebody else’s house.
She said: are you there? and I said I’m here, and she said: is it hot?
I said very.
And she said: put a wet towel on the window if there’s no air. Your grandmother used to. It works.

Which was the least useful advice anybody has ever given me about a two-bedroom apartment in the San Fernando Valley in 2010, and which I have never forgotten, because what she was doing was reaching across eleven thousand kilometres to hand me something. Anything. A towel.
I said I would.
She said: Ali jan. Are you all right.
And I said yes.
I have said yes to that question, in that voice, several hundred times over eleven years, and I want to note, this early, before anything else has happened, that I do not believe I was ever lying.
2. THE CALL — the woman in the forest
She started it about two weeks in, and she did not announce it and she did not ask if I wanted it, which is how everything of any importance has ever been given to me.
She said: do you know how Siavash [see-yaa-VASH] begins?
I said I know the fire.
She said: everybody knows the fire. Nobody knows the beginning and the beginning is the whole thing.

There were two young men out hunting in the forest, she said. Tus [TOOS] and Giv [GEEV]. Great men, famous men, the kind the poem is full of. And they had gone further out than they meant to, into a forest on the border, and in that forest they found a girl.

She was asleep, or she was hiding. She was extraordinarily beautiful and she was alone and she was very well dressed and she was in a forest on the border between two countries that had been at war for a hundred years.
They asked her who she was.

And my mother, who is an art historian and who has spent her whole life looking at things properly, said: pay attention to what she tells them, Ali, because she is a girl on her own in a forest and she is going to say whatever keeps her alive.
She said her father had beaten her. She said her family were Turanian nobility. She said she had run away in the night.
And she gave a name, and the name was from the enemy side, and the two young men understood in about four seconds that this girl was worth something to somebody.
So they fought over her. Actually fought — swords out, in the forest, two of the great heroes of Iran, over which of them found her first and therefore which of them owned her.
And they were still fighting when somebody sensible said: take her to the King.
So they took her to Kavus [kaa-VOOS]. And Kavus looked at her and did what kings did, which is that he kept her.

She was married into the royal house of a country she had been at war with, by men who had been arguing over her ownership an hour earlier, and nobody at any point asked her a question she was not required to answer correctly.
She said: and she had a son.
She said: and he was so beautiful that when they brought him out, the whole court went quiet.
And then she said — and she said it plainly, without weight, and it took me eleven years to hear what she had put in my hands:
And then she was gone from the story. That’s all. She isn’t mentioned again. She has a son and she disappears out of the poem and Ferdowsi [fer-dow-SEE] does not tell you what happened to her.
She said: he is a boy of enemy blood in the palace of his father’s country, and the one person in the world who was from where he was from is not there any more.
I was lying on a foam mattress in Van Nuys with the phone on my chest and I said: that’s a bad start.
And my mother laughed and said: it’s a Persian start. Everything of ours begins with somebody being taken somewhere.
And then she said: are you eating?
3. THE YEARS — eight days
I had a job in eight days and I have never once let anybody make that sound like a virtue, because it was not one. It was fear, professionally applied.

The car wash was on Sepulveda and it was called Sunshine Auto Spa and it was run by an Armenian man named Vartan who had been in the country since 1988 and who hired me in about ninety seconds, in a mixture of two languages, on a Tuesday.
He looked at my hands.

That is the first thing that happened to me in American employment. He took my right hand and turned it over and looked at the palm and looked at me and said nothing at all, and then said: you can grip?
I said yes.
He said: show me.
And I gripped his hand, hard, with the hand that closes about eighty per cent, and he nodded and said be here at seven and that was the entire interview.

He never mentioned it again. Not once, in the two years I worked for him. I have thought about Vartan a great deal and I think what happened in that ninety seconds is that a man who had arrived here at thirty-one with his own history looked at a twenty-one-year-old with something wrong with his hands and made a decision not to require an explanation.

That was my introduction to this country and it was, I want to say, extremely representative. People here will let you be from nowhere. They will let you have arrived fully formed at twenty-one with two scars and no past, and they will not ask, and it is the single greatest gift on offer and it is also, if you are a certain sort of person, a very comfortable place to hide.
Eleven dollars an hour and tips. Seven to four, six days.

The work was: pull the car through, wipe, wheels, glass, move. It was hot and repetitive and I was extremely good at it within about a week, and I need to be honest about why, and the honest reason is that I had spent six years of my adolescence doing a coordinated physical thing in a row of men for four hours at a stretch and my body knew how to do that.
I did not think about it that way at the time. At the time I thought I was just a hard worker.

I saved with a specific and slightly deranged discipline. Four hundred a month to Farhad for the floor and then the room, food that I cooked, no car for the first year, buses everywhere, and everything else went into an envelope and then into an account.
The number was community college and then transfer, and I had worked it out on paper on the plane.
I want to put down what that year was actually like, because there is a version of the immigrant year that gets told and it is either misery or triumph and mine was neither.

It was: getting up at half five. The bus on Sepulveda with the windows open. Nine hours in the sun. The specific pleasure of a cold drink at four in the afternoon when you have been outside since seven. Coming home and cooking rice badly and then better. Learning the freeway names the way you learn the names of streets in a poem. A library card. The enormous quiet of a Sunday when you know nobody.
And a kind of happiness I had never had access to before in my life, which was the happiness of nobody knowing who I was.

Nobody in Los Angeles knew what my father’s silence sounded like across a dinner table, or that my grandfather had died with a word in his mouth that nobody in the family used. Nobody knew about the north or the south of a city eleven thousand kilometres away. Nobody knew what a heyat [hey-AT] was, or whose son I was, or whose grandson, or what had happened to my hands.
I was twenty-one and completely unwitnessed and I have never felt lighter in my life.
4. THE CALL — the man who raised him
She said: so they gave the baby away.
I said what?
She said: not away. Kavus looked at his son and understood — and this is the only clever thing that man does in the entire poem — he understood that he was not capable of raising him.
So he sent for Rostam [ros-TAM].

She had to explain Rostam to me, or she pretended to, which was her way of telling a story properly. Rostam is the great one. The enormous one. Six hundred years old by some counts, the strongest man alive, the one every Iranian child can draw. He came down from Zabolestan [zaa-bo-les-TAAN] and looked at this baby and said: give him to me.
And he took him home and he raised him.
She said: and this is my favourite part of the whole poem and nobody ever quotes it.
She said: Ferdowsi lists what he taught him.

Riding. The bow. The lasso. How to sit at a table. How to speak in an assembly. How to hunt. Wine and the correct behaviour around it. Falconry. Justice — actual justice, how to hear a case and decide it. How to be a guest. How to be a host.
She said: he taught him everything a man needs and he taught it to him personally, for years, and Ferdowsi says that Siavash learned all of it so completely that there was nothing left to teach.
She said: and then the boy said, I want to see my father.
I said: and Rostam let him go?
She said: Rostam took him himself. Rode with him the whole way and delivered him to the palace and presented him.
She said: and the court went mad for him. He was seventeen or so and he was the most accomplished young man anybody had ever seen and everyone said so, out loud, constantly.
And then she said the thing.
She said: and Kavus was delighted with him. Absolutely delighted. He had a son who had come back perfect.
She said: and I want you to notice, Ali, that Kavus is delighted with a thing that another man made.
There was a pause on the line and it was one of the ones where I can hear her deciding whether to say something.
She said: your father says something about you and Amir [a-MEER]. He said it again on Thursday, to the television.
I said what.
She said: he said Amir came out finished and you came out with instructions.
And she laughed, and I laughed, and it was a nice moment and I got off the phone about four minutes later and went to work.
I did not ask her what he meant. I was twenty-one and I had a shift.
I have had eleven years to ask her and I have never once done it.
5. THE YEARS — the first one who remembered
I started at Valley College in the autumn of 2011 with fifteen months of car wash money and a plan that fitted on one side of a piece of paper.

The plan was: two years, transfer, work through both. I did not deviate from it once and I want to be careful about how I say that, because it sounds like discipline and I have come to think it was closer to superstition. I had a piece of paper with a sequence on it and I followed the sequence the way you follow a rite. Do it exactly and something happens. Miss a step and it does not.
Nobody taught me to think like that. Or rather, somebody did, for ten nights a year, for six years, and I did not connect the two things until I was thirty-three and standing in a parking lot.

The first class I loved was a survey course and the professor was a woman named Diane Okafor who taught the nineteenth century and who had, as far as I could tell, no interest whatsoever in whether we liked her.
Third week she handed back a paper of mine with about four hundred words on the back of it. Four hundred. On a two-page assignment from a community college student in his second month.
And what she had written, mostly, was: this is not the argument you think you are making, and the one you are actually making is more interesting, and you seem not to have noticed you were making it.
I read it on the bus and then I read it again standing up at my stop and I missed the stop.
She kept me back after the next class and asked me where I was from and I said Iran and she said no, where did you learn — and made a gesture at the paper — this.
And I said nowhere.
Which was true and was also the biggest lie I told in my first three years in this country, and I told it without any awareness of telling it, which is the kind I have come to be most careful about.
Because the honest answer was: in a walled yard behind a butcher’s shop in south Tehran, from a man with a microphone, on ten consecutive nights a year, from the age of nine.

That is where I learned to build something slowly and hold a room and put the weight in the right place and stop the instant before you have said too much. I learned structure from the rowzeh [row-ZEH]. I learned that you take one small hour and stay inside it for twenty minutes. I learned that the whole craft is knowing when to stop building.
I told a professor at Valley College that I had learned it nowhere, and I believed myself.

She remembered my name. That was the thing. Two hundred students and she remembered my name in the second week and used it, and I went back to a room in Van Nuys that night and sat on the edge of a bed and felt something I did not have a word for.
I have a word for it now and the word is embarrassing. The word is seen.

For six years of my adolescence four hundred men had watched me every winter and I had thought that was being seen and it was not, it was being looked at, which is a different thing entirely and which I had confused with the first thing for my entire life.
A woman I had spoken to twice read two pages and told me what I was actually doing.
I would have done anything for her. I mean that in a completely unromantic way. I would have carried furniture.
6. THE CALL — the queen
She called on a Friday and she had her serious voice and I thought something had happened at home and instead she said: are you sitting down? Because this one is unpleasant.
I said I’m at work.
She said: then I’ll do it badly. Sudabeh [soo-daa-BEH].

Sudabeh was Kavus’s wife. She had come to him out of a war too — everybody in this poem comes out of a war — and she had been loyal to him in a way that cost her, and Ferdowsi is not simple about her. That matters. My mother was extremely firm about it. She is not a monster in the text. She is a woman in a palace with no power except one kind.
And she saw Siavash come home at seventeen from Rostam’s house, finished, beautiful, admired by everyone, and she wanted him.

She said: she manoeuvred. Properly, patiently, over months. She got him brought into the women’s quarters on legitimate business. She arranged to be alone with him. She said things that could be taken two ways so that he would have to decide how to take them, which is the oldest trap there is.
And he refused her. Politely, every time. He was seventeen and he had been raised by Rostam and he had been taught how to be a guest, and he behaved perfectly.
She said: and that is what finished him. If he had been rude she might have let it go. He was correct, and being correct at somebody is the most humiliating thing you can do to them.
So she went to the king.
She tore her own clothes and scratched her own face and went to Kavus and said: your son came for me.
And my mother said, on a Friday, from a kitchen in Elahieh [e-laa-hee-YEH], in a completely level voice:

She said: now. Kavus is not a fool in this moment. That is the part people miss. He investigates. He smells their clothes — that is actually in the poem, he smells them both — and he works out within a day that his wife is lying.
She said: and it changes nothing.
I said what?

She said: he knows she is lying and he still cannot let it go. Because now the court has heard it. Because now there are two versions in the air and one of them is about his son and one is about his wife and he has to be seen to do something.
She said: it stopped being about the truth about eleven minutes after it started.
I was standing in the corridor outside the break room at the car wash and I did not say anything for a moment, and she said: Ali?
And I said: sorry. Bad signal.
There was no bad signal.

I did not know why the number bothered me. I want that on the record. It was 2012 and I was twenty-three and a woman I love said a perfectly ordinary phrase on the telephone and something in my chest turned over and I attributed it to the fact that I had not eaten since six.
7. THE YEARS — the second day
The apartment was mine in 2012. A studio in Van Nuys, second floor, a window that faced a wall.

That was also the spring my parents stopped. I have written about it elsewhere and I am not going to do it again here, except to say that my mother told me on a Friday, in the level voice, from the kitchen, and that my father packed two suitcases and left an apartment that had never in any legal sense been his, and that when I carried a bed frame up two flights alone three weeks later I was thinking, without deciding to, about a man of fifty-two carrying two suitcases down eight floors because he would not, that morning, use the lift he had put in himself.
I did four things in the first forty-eight hours and I am going to list them, because I have listed them to myself perhaps a hundred times since and there is only one that matters.
I bought a bed frame from a man on Craigslist and carried it up alone in two trips.
I put down a rug. It was not a good one. It was the idea of a rug.
I called my mother and walked her around it on the phone, describing the rooms, and she said is there light? four separate times and I kept saying yes and she kept not believing me.
And on the second day I took down the light in the back hallway and put up a different one.

The one that was there was a bare bulb in a wire cage. A cheap outdoor-style fixture that somebody had put on an interior wall because it was what they had. It worked perfectly. There was nothing wrong with it.

I stood in that hallway with my bag still half unpacked and looked at it for I do not know how long and then I went to the hardware store on Victory and bought a flush ceiling fixture with a frosted glass cover for eleven dollars and changed it that afternoon.
I remember being pleased with myself. I remember thinking it looked better.
I did not think about it again for nine years.
There is one more thing about that apartment and it is small.

I never got a proper table. I ate on the floor for the whole two years I was there — a cloth down, the plate on the cloth, sitting cross-legged with my back against the sofa — and when Farhad came over he laughed at me about it, and I laughed too and said I hadn’t got round to it.
I had eleven hundred dollars in an account. I could have got round to it in an afternoon.
My mother, when I told her, said: sofreh [sof-REH]. And I said what, and she said: that is what it is called, when you put the cloth down. You know that.
And I said I know, Maman.
She said: your grandmother did it her whole life and she had four tables.
8. THE CALL — the fire
She called at four in the morning my time.
She did that maybe twice a year and she always had a reason ready and the reason was never the reason. This time the reason was a photograph.
I was twenty-four and I had a shift at seven and I sat up in the dark on the edge of a bed in Van Nuys and said, Maman, it’s four in the morning here.
She said: is it?
And we both let that stand.
She said: it’s you at the aquarium. You’re about five. You’re furious.
I said: I don’t remember an aquarium.

She said: you were furious because you wanted to stay in front of one fish and Amir wanted to keep walking. You stood in front of that glass for forty minutes. Your father wanted to move you and I said leave him.
She said: you have your hands behind your back like a little man. You look like an inspector.

And then she went quiet, and I could hear the room she was in — that specific acoustic of an apartment in Elahieh at four in the morning, which I had not stood in for two and a half years and would know anywhere on earth.
She said: I’ve been sitting with it a while.
I said: Maman, it’s the middle of the night.
She said: I know.
Then, straight into it, no join, the way she has always done it: do you want to hear about the fire?
And I lay back down with the phone on the pillow and said yes.
She said: they built a mountain.

Two hundred camel-loads of wood, she said. Stacked in two great walls with a road between them wide enough for a horse. And they poured naphtha over all of it and they lit it, and the fire went up so high that the whole city came out to watch. So high that the people at the back could feel it on their faces. The smoke had a mountain of its own. It went black over the palace in the middle of the day.
She said: and then they brought out a boy on a black horse.
I could hear her getting up. A woman of fifty-four crossing a room she has lived in for twenty-two years. A cupboard. Water.
She said: he wore white.

She said: he had put on a white robe and a camphor crown, which is what they dressed the dead in, because he had decided that if he was going to be found guilty he would at least go into it dressed correctly.
She said: and he rode up to the fire and got down and went to his father.
And in front of the whole city, she said, he kissed his father’s hand.
I did not say anything.
She said: and he said, don’t be sad. This is what heaven wanted. If I am innocent I will come out. If I am not, then this is what should happen to me.
She said: and Kavus — and Ali, listen to me — his father did not stop it.
She said it very gently. She was not making a point. She was a woman of fifty-four telling her son a story she had known since she was nine.
She said: the boy gave him one last chance, standing in front of a fire the size of a hill, with the whole city watching, and he kissed his hand.
And his father let him get back on the horse.
She stopped.
I could hear her drinking water. I could hear a car go past on a street I grew up on.
She said: are you cold there? It gets cold at night, doesn’t it.
I said it’s fine, Maman.
She said: you never had enough on. Even here. You’d go out in Esfand [es-FAND] in that thin jacket and I’d shout and you’d stand in the doorway with your face like that.
She said: I still think about that. Isn’t that stupid. Of everything.
I said: what happened in the fire.
She said: he rode straight into the middle of it and he was gone a long time. Long enough that people were weeping. Long enough that his father started to understand what he had done.
She said: and then he came out on the other side.

She said: and there was not a mark on him. Not on the robe, not on the horse, not on the crown. He came out of two hundred camel-loads of burning wood with his white clothes still white and Ferdowsi says he was smiling.
I said: so he was fine.
And my mother, eleven thousand kilometres away, at half past four in the afternoon, in the apartment I grew up in, said:
No, my love. He was proved. That’s a different thing.

She said: the city went mad. They shouted for three days. His father wept on his neck and gave him gold and horses and begged him. Sudabeh should have died for it and Siavash asked that she be spared, because he was that sort of person.
She said: and after all of it — after the fire, after the proof, after three days of shouting — nothing in that house was ever the same again.
She said: his father had let him ride into it. And they both knew.
She said: you can be proved innocent in front of an entire city, Ali, and still have to live in the house afterwards.
I did not say anything for a while.
And she said, into the silence, in a completely different voice — the practical one, the one I would know in a crowd of ten thousand people:
Are you eating? Properly. Not the bread and the cheese. Properly.
I said yes.
She said: I don’t believe you. I’m going to send you the advieh [ad-vee-YEH], the one you like. I’ll give it to Mrs Kazemi’s daughter, she’s going in Khordad [khor-DAAD].
I said: Maman, you can buy it here. There’s a shop on Westwood that has everything.
And she said: it isn’t the same one.
And we both knew it was exactly the same one, and neither of us said so, because what she meant was let me put something in your hands from here, and there is no way to say that and no need.
I said: I have to sleep, Maman. It’s nearly five.
She said: all right.
She said: Ali jan.
I said: yes.

And she said — and this is the part I have thought about most, and it took me until I was thirty-three to understand what she had been handing me one piece at a time for eleven years without either of us knowing:
She said: you know you don’t have to prove anything to me. Don’t you. You never did. Not once, not ever, not for one single day.
And I said: I know, Maman.
And she said: I don’t think you do.

I lay in the dark for the fifty minutes I had left before the alarm and did not sleep and did not cry, and was not aware of not crying, and got up at ten to six and washed my face and went to work and had a fine day.
PART TWO — THE GOOD YEARS
9. THE YEARS — the hair

I grew my hair in 2013 and I kept it for two years and I want to explain what that actually was, because from the outside it is a young man in Los Angeles growing his hair, which is the least interesting event in the history of that city.

In Tehran I had a haircut. Not a style — a haircut, the one, the one every boy in my school had, because the alternative was a conversation. Short at the sides, a bit on top, done every six weeks by a man called Naser who had done my father’s hair and who did not ask what I wanted because there was nothing to ask.
I did not object to it. It never occurred to me to object to it. That is the part I could not have explained to anybody here.
And then I was twenty-four in a country where nobody knew me and I simply did not go to the barber.

That was the whole decision. It was not a decision. It was an absence of one, for four months, and then one morning I was standing in a bathroom in Van Nuys pulling it back off my face with one hand and I looked at myself and thought: oh.
By the end of that year it was past my shoulders and I looked like somebody else.

A man at a bus stop on Victory once told me I looked like a Sufi who had got into a band. My brother, on video from Toronto, laughed for a full minute and then said, in Persian, Maman is going to have a stroke, and my mother did not have a stroke, she said: it’s nice. You’ve got your grandfather’s hair. Not the Perspolis [pers-PO-lis] one. The other one. My father, from a lawn chair in Irvine, looked at the screen for four full seconds and then asked whether I was eating.
Then the ring.

A septum ring, in 2014, from a place on Melrose, done by a woman with grey hair and forearms covered in ink who talked me through it like a nurse. It hurt more than I expected and my eyes ran and she said everyone’s do.

I had it for about fourteen months. Then gauges in my ears for about eight, which were a mistake and which left me with two small permanent slack places that I am mildly embarrassed by. Then I took all of it out at once, in one evening, and never put any of it back.

There was a vegan year. There was a band, which was bad, in which I played bass adequately and wrote nothing. There was a period of about five months in which I wore only black, which is funny for reasons that took me a long time to find funny.
Here is what I want on the record about all of it, because I have heard other people from where I am from describe this badly.

I was not rebelling. There was nothing to rebel against. My mother thought the hair was nice. My brother thought it was funny. My father asked if I was eating. Nobody in Los Angeles cared at all — that is the entire point of Los Angeles, it is a city with an infinite tolerance for a man reinventing himself in public, and it will not applaud you for it either.
What I was doing was much stranger and much more boring than rebellion.
I was finding out what I was like.

I had been fifteen and had a personality assembled out of oppositions. My grandfather was red so I was blue. My family was secular so I went south. My brother was easy so I was the difficult one. Every single thing I was, I was against something, and that works perfectly well as a structure and it means you have never once found out what you would choose in an empty room.
I was twenty-four and alone in a room the size of a country and nobody was on the other side of anything.

So I tried things on. Most of them did not fit. Some of them fitted so badly that I still think about them. And the astonishing thing, the thing I was not prepared for, was that it did not matter. Nothing was lost. You could be a vegan with long hair and a septum ring for a year and then not be, and no one held it against you, and there was no committee.
I have never been able to make anybody from home understand how enormous that is.
10. THE CALL — and it changed nothing
She left it a long time. Months. And when she came back to it she did it the way she does, which is mid-sentence, from somewhere else.
She was telling me about a leak in the bathroom and the man who came to look at it and then she said: do you know what happened after the fire?
I said: he was proved.
She said: yes. And nothing happened.
She said: for a little while it was glorious. Three days of the city shouting. Gold. Horses. His father weeping on his neck.
And then everybody went back to what they were doing.

She said: and the whispering did not stop. That is the thing nobody tells you about being proved. Sudabeh was still in the palace. She had asked for him and been refused and been humiliated and been publicly caught, and she was still there, at dinner, every night, and she had not been punished because Siavash had asked that she be spared.

She said: so she started again. Quieter this time. Sorcery, in the poem — she hires people, there are potions, there is a business with a dead child that I am not going to describe to you at eleven o’clock at night.
She said: and the court listened. Not because they believed her. Because it was interesting.
I said: but he walked through a fire.
And my mother said: Ali. Nobody in the history of the world has ever been argued out of a thing they enjoyed believing.
She said: the fire proved he did not do it. It did not stop people saying he did. Those are separate systems and the second one does not care about the first one at all.
She said: and the worst of it was in his own house.

Because Kavus knew. He had smelled the clothes, he had watched his son ride into two hundred camel-loads of burning wood in a white robe, and he had let him do it, and now he had to sit across a table from him every evening.
She said: a man who has wronged you and knows it is the most dangerous person in your life. Not a man who hates you. A man who owes you and cannot pay.

She said: he started to be able to hardly look at him. And Siavash, who had done nothing, who had been perfect, who had asked for mercy for the woman who tried to destroy him — Siavash started to understand that the price of being right was that his father could not be in a room with him.
I said something like: so he left?
And she said: not yet. First he did what people do, which is he made himself useful. He volunteered for a war.

She said: which is what young men do when a house has stopped being liveable. They find something enormous and honourable to go and do somewhere else, and everyone praises them for it, and nobody asks what they are getting away from.
There was a pause.
She said: is that a siren?
I said: it’s an ambulance. There’s a hospital four blocks over. You get used to it.
And she said: I don’t like that. That you get used to it.
11. THE YEARS — the desert, alone

I went to Joshua Tree by myself in the spring of 2014, in a car I had owned for four months, with a tent I had bought that morning and a cooler with too much in it because I did not know how much a person needs.
I had been in this country four years and I had not once been anywhere without a reason.

That is worth stopping on. Four years of a sequence on a piece of paper — shift, class, shift, sleep — and every single mile I had travelled had been toward an obligation. I did not know how to go somewhere for no reason. It is not a skill you are issued with, where I am from, at least not in the family I am from, and it took me four years to work out that a Saturday was mine.
So I drove east and got there in the afternoon and put up a tent badly and sat on a rock.
The heat went off the ground at about six and by eight it had dropped twenty degrees and I was in every layer I had brought, which was not enough, because I never bring enough.
And the stars came out.
I had not seen stars like that since I was a boy on a road outside Karaj [ka-RAJ] with my father driving and my brother asleep against the window.

I sat in the dark with my back against a rock that was still warm from the day, in the middle of a country I had chosen, and I was — I want to use the correct word — content. Not happy, exactly. Something quieter and better than happy. Alone, warm on one side and cold on the other, with nobody knowing where I was and nobody needing me anywhere until Monday.
And I noticed, after some indeterminate time, that I was making a noise.
Not singing. Barely audible. A rhythm, under my breath, four beats and a stop, four beats and a stop.

The words were gone. Genuinely gone — I could not have told you what they had been. What was left was the metre. Just the shape of the thing, the way a floor keeps the shape of a table that was moved out of a room years ago.
I stopped as soon as I noticed.

I did not think: that is a nowheh [now-HEH]. I did not think anything at all. I stopped the way you stop biting your nails when you catch yourself, with a small flinch of embarrassment and no examination whatsoever, and then I got the cooler and made something to eat.
There was nobody there to ask me what it was.

I have wondered since whether that was lucky. If somebody had been sitting on that rock with me and said what’s that, I would have had to say something, and I would have said nothing, just a song, and I would have heard myself say it.
Nobody was there. So I did not have to lie, and because I did not have to lie, I did not have to notice.
That is the whole of my twenties in one evening in the desert, and I would not have believed you if you had told me.
I drove back Sunday afternoon on the 10 with the windows down and thought it had been one of the best weekends of my life.

It had. That is not sarcasm. I want to be clear that I am not building toward the idea that those years were secretly miserable. They were not. I was twenty-five and free and doing well and I had a Saturday that belonged to me and stars over a rock, and I earned every part of it, and it was real.
The thing about a door is that you can live in the house.
12. THE CALL — the treaty
She said: he took the war and he was extraordinary at it.

Rostam went with him — that is the detail she loved, that the old man came out of Zabolestan again for him — and the two of them went east and they were unstoppable. Balkh [BALKH] taken. City after city. Siavash was about twenty-two and he was doing, publicly and enormously well, the exact thing he had been raised for.
She said: and Afrasiyab [af-raa-see-YAAB], who was the king of Turan [too-RAAN] and who had been Iran’s enemy since before anybody could remember, had a dream.
She said: it is a real dream and it is worth hearing.

He dreamed of a desert full of snakes and an air full of eagles. He dreamed of a wind that pulled up his tent and turned his banner over. He dreamed of a field of severed heads and a throne with a young man on it who looked at him and said: why are you doing this, your time is finished.
He woke up screaming and the room came running.
She said: and he called his advisers and he said, I am going to make peace. Whatever it costs.
So he sent a hundred hostages.
Not soldiers. Sons. The sons of the hundred best families of Turan, handed over into Siavash’s keeping as a guarantee, and with them a message: take these, take the provinces, and let it stop.
And Siavash, who was twenty-two, thought about it and consulted Rostam and accepted.
She said: and everybody who tells this story badly says he was naive.
She said: he was not naive. He got everything. He got the land, he got the hostages, he got the war ended without another dead boy. Any commander in the world would have taken that.
She said: and then he did the thing that killed him, which is that he gave his word.
She said: do you understand what that meant then?

She said: a hundred young men came into his camp because he had said, with his hand, that they would be safe. They slept in his camp. They ate his food. He knew their names. Some of them were sixteen.
She said: it was not a contract. There was no paper. The whole thing was that he had said it.
I said: and his father hated it.
And she said: we’ll get to that.
She said: it’s late here. But I’ll tell you one thing now so you have it.
And she said: the reason this poem is a thousand years old and we are still telling it is not the fire. It is what happens when a young man is asked to choose between his word and his home.
She said: everybody gets asked that. Not with a hundred hostages. But everybody gets asked.
And then she said: are you sleeping properly? You sound thin.
And I said you can’t sound thin, Maman.
And she said: you can.
13. THE YEARS — the phone on a chair
I graduated in the spring of 2015. Twenty-six. Five years from a car wash on Sepulveda to a degree, which is not fast and is not slow and which I did every single day of.
They give you a folding chair in a stadium and it takes four hours and almost all of it is other people’s names.
My mother watched it on a telephone.

Amir flew in from Toronto. That was the arrangement — my mother does not fly, has not since the year I was born, for reasons she has never once explained and I have never once asked about — so my brother came to my graduation as a delegate. My father drove up from Irvine, where he had been since Nowruz, in my aunt’s car, in a jacket, and sat four rows behind Amir and did not say one word for four hours, which for him is a medical event.
And Amir did the thing that I did not know I needed and that I have never properly thanked him for.

He propped his phone against a water bottle on the empty seat beside him, on a video call, for four hours, so that our mother could sit in a kitchen in Elahieh at four in the morning and watch a stadium in the San Fernando Valley from an angle that mostly showed the back of a stranger’s head.

Four hours. She did not go to bed. When they finally got to the S names Amir picked the phone up and held it over the crowd and I could hear her, from about forty metres away, over eleven thousand people, doing the thing that women from where I am from do at weddings.
She said afterwards that she saw me. I have watched that footage. You cannot see me. There is a man in a gown who might be anybody.
She saw me.

Afterwards we ate in a Persian place in Tarzana because Amir wanted to and I did not, and he was right and I was wrong, and the three of us sat in a booth with the phone propped against the sugar and had dinner with our mother, who had not slept, at nine in the morning her time, with a cup of tea, in a kitchen I could see the corner of.
She said: is that khoresh — and then, in English, for the waiter’s benefit, though the waiter was in Tarzana and had not needed English for the last decade: is that the good one?
Amir said: it’s the good one.
She said: Ali jan. Say something.
And I could not think of anything at all, and I said: I did it.
And she said: I know, my love. I was there.
Here is a small thing that I have kept.
My father paid. He made a performance of the bill that Amir still does at parties. He folded the receipt into his shirt pocket, which I noticed, and thought nothing of.

At some point in that dinner my father went outside — to take a call, or to make one, or to stand on Ventura Boulevard with a toothpick and look at the traffic, which is a thing he does — and Amir went with him, and my mother said, in the two minutes we had alone, in a completely ordinary voice:
She said: he was unbearable today, wasn’t he. He told the waiter. I could hear him telling the waiter through a telephone.
She said: Kamran [kam-RAAN] Shabani [sha-baa-NEE], whose son has a degree. He’ll have it in a conversation about parking by Tuesday.
And then she said: you know that, don’t you.
I said yes.
She said: I know you do. I like saying it.
14. THE CALL — the letter
She said: are you sitting down?
I said: you always ask me that and you have never once waited for the answer.
She said: sit down.
She said: Siavash had done everything right.

He had ended a war. He had taken the provinces. He had a hundred hostages in his camp, alive and safe and fed, from the best families of the other side. He had written to his father to tell him it was finished.
She said: and the letter came back.
She said: and I want you to understand that the letter was not angry. It was worse than angry, Ali. It was a father being disappointed.
The letter said: kill them.

It said: send them to me and I will do it, or do it there, it does not matter. There is no peace with that country. You are young and you have been fooled. Burn what you have taken, kill the hostages, and come home.
She said: and there it is. That is all of it. That is what this poem is about, and everybody thinks it is about a fire.
She said: a young man is told, by the person he most wants to be loved by, that the price of coming home is his own word.
There was a silence on the line then. It was costing money and neither of us said anything.
She said: he wrote back and said no.
She said: he said, I gave my hand on it. They came to me under my hand. I will not.

And she said: and that was the door closing. He was twenty-two years old standing in a camp in a foreign country and he had just found out that home was conditional and that he could not meet the condition.
She said: he did not do anything wrong, Ali. I am always careful about this because the story is very old and people tell it badly.
He did not sin. He did not rebel. He did not choose adventure.
He kept his word, exactly as he had been raised to, and it turned out that the man who raised him did not mean it.

She said: so he sent the hostages back to their own families, with an escort, unharmed. He sent the army home to his father with a general in charge of it. He kept about three hundred men who chose to stay.
And then he sat down and thought about where a person goes.
And she said the line, gently, at eleven at night her time:
He went to the enemy. Because they had not lied to him yet.
I did not say anything for long enough that she said my name.
I said: I’m here. It’s the room, there’s an echo.
There was no echo.
She said: all right.
She said: shall I stop?
And I said no. Too fast. I said: no, keep going.

And she did. And I stood in a kitchen in a country that had taken me in and listened to my mother tell me about a young man riding away from everything he came from, with three hundred men, in good faith, toward people who were kind to him for a while.
She said: I’ll do the rest another time. It’s late. Are you eating?
I said yes.
She said: Ali jan.
I said: yes.
She said: I’m proud of you. You know that.
15. THE YEARS — the first thing with my name on it
I need to say what I do, because I have been avoiding it for fourteen chapters the way I avoided it at parties for about six years.
I make things for other people’s buildings.

That is the short version and it is the one I gave strangers for a long time. The longer version is that I ended up in a small studio in Frogtown that does interpretive design — museums, mostly, and civic spaces, and occasionally a lobby for somebody with money who wants the lobby to say something. You are given a room and a subject and a budget and you have to decide what a person is going to understand, in what order, in the eleven minutes they will actually spend there.
Sequence. Pacing. What you show first. What you withhold until the third panel. How long to stay inside one small thing before you move.
I was extremely good at it almost immediately and I told everybody it was luck.
The first job that was mine was in 2016 and it was small — a single room in a county historical society about ninety minutes out, about a labour dispute in the nineteen-twenties that had ended badly.
And what I did with it, which was apparently unusual, was I refused to put the outcome in the first room.

The client wanted the deaths on the entry panel because the deaths are what the room is about. And I said no. I said you put them in and you have told everybody how to feel before they have met anybody. Give me the whole first wall for the men. Names, hours, what they were paid, what a shift was, what they ate. Make somebody stand there for four minutes with people who are alive.
Then the second wall.
They ran it. It won a small regional award that nobody outside the field has heard of and I have the certificate in a drawer and I know exactly where the drawer is.
Diane Okafor came to the opening. She had retired by then. She stood in that first room for a long time and then she said: you built it like a piece of music.
And I said thank you.
She said: where did you learn to withhold like that?
And I said: I don’t know. I just do it.

That is the second time somebody asked me that question and the second time I said nothing, and I gave exactly the same answer, five years apart, in the same tone, and I did not notice that I had said it before.

What I did not say, because I did not know it, was: I learned it from a man on a microphone in a yard in south Tehran who would sit on a low note four times and refuse to give you the high one until the whole room was leaning.
I learned it from a dead man.
I have built a career on a technique I inherited by watching somebody, and I did not find that out until I was thirty-three, and when I did find out I had already been paid for it for six years.
16. THE CALL — the country that was kind
She said: this is the part nobody tells.
She said: everyone knows the fire and everyone knows the ending and the middle is thrown away, and the middle is seven years long.
He crossed the river. That is the moment. He rode over the border into the country his own people had been at war with since before anyone could remember, with three hundred men, and he was met.
Afrasiyab came out to meet him personally, which for a king was enormous, and put his arms around him and wept.

She said: and I do not think he was lying. That is the part that makes this a good poem instead of a simple one. Afrasiyab had had a dream about a young man on a throne telling him his time was finished, and here was the young man, at his gate, with nothing, asking for shelter — and he embraced him and meant it.
She said: people can be genuinely kind to you and it can still end the way it ends. Both things.
She said: he gave him everything.

A province. Horses. A place at his right hand. He watched him play chess and lost and laughed about it. He watched him ride at the polo and could not believe what he was seeing. He gave him his daughter.

Her name was Farangis [fa-raan-GEES], and Ferdowsi does something with her that he almost never does with a woman in that poem, which is that he lets her be right. She is not decoration. She sees what is coming before anybody, she says so out loud, and she is not listened to.
She said: and they were happy.

She said it flatly. She said: I want you to hear that properly because it is not a device. They were happy. Seven years. A marriage that worked. A child coming. He was twenty-three when he crossed and he was thirty when it ended and in between he had the only settled years of his life, in a foreign country, among people who were not his.
I said: he never went home.
And she said: no. And that is not the tragedy either.
She said: the tragedy is not that he was in exile. Plenty of people are in exile and are fine. He built a life. He was loved. He was good at it.
She said: the tragedy is that he was in a place where nothing that had happened to him could be explained.

She said: nobody in that country had been at the fire. Nobody had smelled the clothes. Nobody had read the letter. He was surrounded by people who were kind to him and knew none of it, and he could not tell them, because how do you tell a Turanian that your own father asked you to cut a hundred Turanian boys’ throats and you refused?
She said: so he did not say it. To anybody. For seven years.
I was standing at a window in Frogtown at nine in the evening and I said: Maman, I have to go, I’ve got a thing in the morning.
And she said: all right, my love.
And she said: Ali.
And I said yes.
And she said: nothing. Go on. I’ll call Sunday.
17. THE YEARS — I was happy
I am going to spend a chapter on this because if I do not, the rest of the book will read as though I was building toward something, and I was not. I was living.
It is 2016. I am twenty-seven. Here is the inventory.
A one-bedroom in Frogtown with a lemon tree in the yard that belonged to the building and that I picked from anyway. Rent I could afford. A car that started.

Work I was good at and that mattered a small amount to a small number of people, which is the correct size for work to matter. I could look at a room and know what a stranger would understand in it, and in what order, and I got paid for that.
Money in an account for the first time in my life. Not much. Enough that a bad month was a bad month and not a catastrophe, which is a distinction that people who have always had it cannot feel.

A group of about nine people who I saw regularly and who saw me. Not friends the way I had understood the word at fifteen — nobody in that group would have gone to prison for me. But they knew what I did and remembered my mother’s name and one of them noticed when I shaved my head and said it suited me.

And, for a few months of most years, a father in a lawn chair in Irvine, forty miles south, who could not fit into any apartment I have ever rented and whom I drove down to on the odd Sunday and said nothing to that either of us would remember, and who is barely in this book because he has one of his own.
Sunday mornings. A bakery on Fletcher. Running badly, three times a week, in a park, listening to nothing.

And a thing I did every year in October which was to go to the ocean by myself and stand in it up to the knees for about ten minutes, which I started for no reason and did for eight consecutive years and have never told anybody about until this sentence.
I want to be extremely clear.
I was happy.

Not managing. Not coping. Not building a life around an absence. Happy, in the plain and unremarkable way that most people are happy for stretches of years, and I knew I was, at the time, in the moment, which is rarer than being happy.

I had done what I set out to do at twenty-one standing at an airport barrier with a bag while three hundred people met somebody else. I had made a life out of nothing, alone, in a language I had learned properly on a bus, and there was no part of it I had been given.
That is the thing that makes what comes later possible. Not the misery. The competence.
A man who is falling apart gets found. A man who is doing extremely well does not, because there is nothing to find, and everybody around him has excellent evidence that he is fine, and so does he.
My mother said, on the phone in that year: you sound settled.
And I said I am.
And she said: good. That’s all I wanted.
And then, after a moment, in the tone she uses when she is putting something down on a table between us rather than handing it to me:
She said: you were such a serious little boy. You have no idea. You’d sit on the step of the building with your chin on your hands like a man waiting for a bus that was late.
She said: I used to think, what is he thinking about. And I’d ask, and you’d say nothing.
She said: and I believed you. That’s the part. You were four and I believed you.
18. THE CALL — the city he built
She said: he built a city.
She said it the way you would announce a birth.
Afrasiyab gave him land — a whole province, out toward the east — and Siavash went there and did not sit in it. He built.

She said: two cities. The first one was called Gang Dezh [GANG DEZH], the fortress-town, and the second one was Siavashgerd [see-yaa-vash-GERD], which just means the place Siavash made, and Ferdowsi spends real time on it, which he almost never does.

Gardens. Watercourses. A palace with painted rooms — and this is the part my mother could not get through without stopping — he had them paint the walls of that palace with the kings of Iran. His own family. His father. The whole line, in a hall, in a foreign country, painted by Turanian craftsmen who had never seen any of them.
She said: he built a room to be homesick in.
I said: that’s a lot for a man who was fine.
And she said: he was fine. That’s what I keep saying to you. He was fine and he painted his father on a wall in another country. Both.
She said: and Farangis wanted a child, and everybody knew it.
And she said: and this is where it starts, and it starts with somebody visiting.
Afrasiyab sent his own brother to see the new city. A man called Garsivaz [gar-see-VAAZ].
And Garsivaz arrived and was shown around. The gardens, the watercourses, the painted hall. The polo ground. The people, who liked him. The wife, who was the king’s daughter. A child talked about.
She said: and Ferdowsi tells you exactly what happened inside that man in one line. He says: his heart filled with envy.
That is all. No plot yet, no scheme. A man walked around a beautiful place that a younger man had made and something turned over in him, and he went home with it.
She said: I want you to understand how ordinary this is.
She said: Sudabeh needed a whole apparatus. Sorcery, a hired woman, a dead child, a public accusation. All of it failed. He walked out of a mountain of fire without a mark.
She said: Garsivaz needed nothing at all. He needed to be believed slightly, by one person, over a long period.
She said: the fire could not touch him and a man talking quietly at dinner killed him in eighteen months.
I said: what did he say?

And she said: small things. Always small. That is the technique and it has not changed in a thousand years. He never said Siavash is plotting. He said things that were true and arranged them badly. He said, the men love him. He said, they say his name before yours in that province. He said, he writes letters. He said, he is your enemy’s son and he has your daughter and a child coming and an army that likes him and a city with your rivals painted on the wall.
Every single one of those was true.
She said: he did not lie once, Ali. He just chose what to mention.
I was in the kitchen in Frogtown with the window open and I said: that’s —
And I did not finish it, because I did not have the end of the sentence.
She said: what?
I said: nothing. Someone’s dog.
She said: all right, my love.
She said: I’ll do the rest another time. It gets bad now.
PART THREE — PREFERENCES
19. THE YEARS — I left a wedding
It was 2017 and it was somebody from work and it was in a hotel in Pasadena and I had been looking forward to it for a month.
I was fine through the ceremony and fine through the dinner and fine for the first part of the dancing, which I do badly and enjoy anyway.

And then they did the thing they do at those weddings, which is that everybody got in a circle and put their arms around each other’s shoulders and began to move together, side to side, on the beat, all at the same time.
Maybe sixty people.
I got out of the circle.
I did it politely, with the face you make — bathroom — and I went out through the lobby and stood in the parking structure for about twenty minutes.
My heart rate was, I would estimate, a hundred and forty. My hands were wet. There was a very specific thing happening in my chest that I would describe as a machine trying to start.
And I stood between two cars in a parking structure in Pasadena and I thought, with complete sincerity: I really do not like crowds.
I want to sit inside that sentence for a second because it is the most useful thing in this book.

It was not a lie. I was not concealing anything from myself in any sense that a psychologist would recognise. I had a physical event, I looked for a cause, I found one that fitted perfectly well and was socially available and required nothing from me, and I filed it.
I don’t like crowds. Thousands of people don’t. Nobody has ever once been asked to justify it.

I used that sentence for nine years — I had been using it since 2012, it turned out; the wedding was only the first time I heard myself. I used it on my mother. I used it at a work thing in 2018 and a man said me neither and we had a nice conversation about it.
Here is what I know now that I did not know then, and it is not dramatic and there was no way for me to have found it out.
It was not the crowd. I have been in enormous crowds and been fine. I have been at a concert with fourteen thousand people and had the time of my life.
It was the unison. It was sixty people moving at the same time on the same beat with their arms on each other’s shoulders.
That is a different thing entirely, and there is no word for it in English, and so for nine years I used the nearest available word and it was the wrong one.

That is how it works. You do not get a locked door with a sign on it. You get a slightly wrong word that fits well enough, and then you build a personality on top of it, and the personality is load-bearing and completely sincere.
I went back in after twenty minutes and had a good night and got home at two and thought nothing about it at all.
I want that in the record.
Thought nothing about it at all.
20. THE CALL — the man at dinner
She did not come back to it for two months and when she did she started somewhere I did not expect.
She said: do you know what happened to Sudabeh in the end?
I said no.
She said: nothing. She is barely mentioned again. She does one enormous evil thing, it fails completely, and then she is furniture until somebody kills her offstage years later.
She said: that is Ferdowsi being honest. The person who tries hardest to destroy him is not the one who does it.
She said: Garsivaz went home and worked for eighteen months.
She said: and I want to describe the method properly because you will meet it.

He did not accuse. He withheld and implied. He would come back from the east and say very little, and when the king asked how it was, he would say it was fine, and pause slightly too long, and change the subject.
She said: a pause is not a lie. Nobody can hold you to a pause.
She said: and Afrasiyab, who had loved that boy, who had come out to the border and put his arms around him and wept — Afrasiyab started to sleep badly.
She said: and then Garsivaz did the second half, which is the part that made me put the book down when I was nineteen.
He went east again. And he went to Siavash and he said: be careful. The king is turning against you.
She said: he ran it from both ends. He made the king afraid of the boy and the boy afraid of the king, and then all he had to do was let the two of them behave normally.
She said: because a frightened man’s ordinary behaviour looks exactly like guilt. Siavash started keeping his men closer. Perfectly reasonable. And Garsivaz reported it.
I said: did nobody see it?
And she said: Farangis saw it. She saw all of it. She told him.
She said: she said to him — she was pregnant, she was the king’s daughter, she knew that court — she said, do not go to my father. Whatever the letter says, do not go.
She said: and he went.
I said: why?
And my mother was quiet for a moment and then she said the thing that I did not understand for another four years:
She said: because he had spent his whole life being able to prove he was innocent, and he had never once considered that it might not help.

She said: he thought if he stood in front of the man and explained it, it would be all right. He had walked through a fire. He had a system, my love. And the system had worked once, spectacularly, in front of a whole city, and he had never noticed that afterwards nothing changed.
She said: how are you sleeping?
I said fine.
She said: you always say fine.
I said because I’m always fine.
And she laughed and said: that is exactly what your father says. Every day. In writing.
21. THE YEARS — the playlist
I have a playlist called slow and it has about ninety things on it and I made it in 2017 and I still use it.

It is what I put on in the car, at work, running, cooking. People have commented on it. A woman I dated briefly in 2018 said my music taste was very deliberate, which she meant as an observation and which I took as a compliment.
I built it over about a year by removing things.
Here is how the removing worked, and I did not describe it this way at the time because I did not have this way to describe it.

Something would come on and I would not enjoy it. Not dislike — that is too strong and too conscious. I would notice a small unpleasantness, a slight leaning-away, and I would skip it. And after a while I would stop putting that artist on. And after a longer while the whole area would quietly close.

Anything with a four-on-the-floor kick at a certain speed. Anything with a hand-clap on the two and the four at a certain speed. Anything in a gym. Most dance music of any era. Two entire decades of Iranian pop that my brother loves and that my mother had in the car when I was small.
I told people I liked things slow. I told people I found that stuff exhausting. I said the word exhausting a great many times over nine years and I believed it every time.
In 2021, after everything, I sat down at a table with a tap-tempo app and went through the playlist properly, because by then I needed to know.
The playlist averages ninety-four beats per minute. Nothing on it goes above a hundred and eighteen.

And the things I had removed — the things I could not be in a room with, the things that made me leave a gym and cancel a membership I had paid for — sat, almost without exception, between about a hundred and twenty-five and a hundred and thirty-five.

There is a number in the middle of that range and I am not going to write it again in this chapter because I have written it enough for one lifetime, and because the point is not that I avoided one number.

The point is that a man built a nine-year aesthetic preference out of a window about ten beats wide, told everybody it was taste, and was so convincing about it that he convinced himself, and that the whole thing was completely invisible from the inside and would have stayed invisible for the rest of his life if a nineteen-year-old had not looked at him in a garage in Highland Park.
I want to say one more thing about the playlist and it is the part that I find hardest.
It is a good playlist.

It is genuinely, actually good. People ask me for it. I have given it to about eleven people. There is nothing wrong with any of the ninety things on it and I love them and I chose them and they are mine.
The door does not make you worse. That is what nobody says. It just quietly decides some things for you, and the things it decides are usually fine, and you get to keep the credit.
22. THE CALL — she stopped
She stopped for two years.

I do not think she did it deliberately. I want to be careful there, because it would be very easy for me, from here, to build my mother into somebody who was managing me, and she was not. She was a woman of sixty in Tehran with a bad knee and a leaking bathroom and a son eleven thousand kilometres away.
But she stopped, and I noticed, and I never once said anything.
She had left it at Garsivaz. At the man talking quietly at dinner and the letters going both ways.

And after that the calls kept coming — Sundays, mostly, plus the four in the mornings — and they were about the knee, and the bathroom, and Mrs Kazemi’s daughter, and whether I was eating. All the ordinary machinery of a mother and a son on two continents.
And every so often I would say: what happened after that?
And she would say: oh, it’s grim. I’ll do it when I’m in the mood.
Twice she started and stopped.
Once she got as far as the letter — Afrasiyab’s letter summoning him — and then said, actually, no, not tonight, I’ve had a day.
And once, in the winter of 2018, she got further. She got him onto the horse. She got him riding out with three hundred men to go and explain himself to a man who had already decided.
And then she said: he took the road along the river.
And there was a pause of about four seconds and then she said, in a completely different voice: did I tell you the Kazemis are thinking of selling?
I let her.
That is the whole of my part in this. I let her, for two years, without ever once saying Maman, why do you keep stopping.
And I have gone round and round on why I did that, and the honest answer is not noble. It is not that I was being gentle with her.
It is that I did not want the end of the story either.
I have never been able to work out how much of that was for her sake. I would like to report that it was mostly for her sake. I do not think it was.
She came back to it in 2021. Once, at the end, all in one go, and she did it because I asked her to, and I asked her because by then I had to.

But there were two years in the middle where a woman in Elahieh and a man in Frogtown both quietly agreed not to get to the part where the young man dies, and neither of us ever mentioned the agreement, and I am not sure either of us knew we had made one.
That is the most Iranian thing in this book.
23. THE YEARS — the interview
The interview was in 2019 in a federal building downtown and it took eleven minutes and I had prepared for it for four months.

The officer was a man in his fifties with a very clean desk. He was not unkind. I want to say that clearly because there is a version of this story that people expect and it is not what happened. He was professional, slightly bored, and entirely reasonable.
He asked me the questions. I answered them. My file was in good order because I had spent nine years making sure my file was in good order.
And then he asked me to sign something and I put my hand out for the pen.
And he stopped.
Not dramatically. He looked at my hand on his desk for perhaps a second and a half longer than a person looks at a hand.
Then he wrote something. Two words, maybe three. On a form, in a box, with a government pen.
And then he said: any history of self-harm?
I said no.
He said: all right. And he moved on and I signed the thing and eleven minutes later I was in an elevator.
Here is what I want to describe, because it is the closest this book comes to a crime and no crime occurred.

He was doing his job. There is a box. It is there for good reasons, put there by people trying to help. A man came in with two matched scars across both palms, of a kind that is genuinely, statistically associated with one particular thing, and the officer noticed it, and asked, and recorded the answer.
He did everything correctly.
And I said no, which was true, and which he wrote down, and which will now sit in a file in this country forever next to two words I did not read and cannot request.
I could have explained.
That is the thing. There was no rule against it. He would probably have listened. It would have taken ninety seconds.
I fell forward onto a blade lying on wet concrete during a scuffle in a yard in Tehran when I was fifteen.
And then he would have said: what were you doing in the yard?

And there it is. That is the whole architecture. You cannot tell the small true thing without the large true thing behind it, and the large true thing was a banned rite and eleven men in a yard and a name that forty families in south Tehran have spent twenty years not saying.
So I said no.

I have said no to that question, in one form or another, to a doctor, to a nurse, to a physiotherapist, twice to women, once to a man at a pool, and every single time it was true, and every single time it was the least honest thing I have ever said.

I got citizenship in 2020. My mother cried on the phone. Amir sent something ridiculous. My father, who had had the same passport in a drawer for fifteen years and never once used it for anything but a stamp, said nothing for a while, and then said: good, now they can’t send you back either. Which was a joke, and was not. I framed nothing and I told nobody at work for a fortnight and I could not have told you why.
24. THE YEARS — what my uncle said
My uncle Mehran [meh-RAAN] died in the winter of 1387, which is 2009, which was fourteen months before I left.

He died of his lungs, which had been killing him since 1366, which is to say he died of an afternoon in a marsh at twenty years old over the following twenty-one years, on an instalment plan, in a country that had given him a medal for it.
Eleven days at the end. I was there for all of them and I am not going to write about it here.
But there is a thing he said and I need to put it down now, in its correct place, in the middle of a chapter about ordinary memory, because that is exactly how I carried it for twelve years.
It was day eight or nine. He was on the oxygen and he had gone past the point of arranging things, which is the point where people say what they actually have.
I was on a chair. He said my name.
And then he said: you were at the corner.
I said what?
And he said — and it took him a while, it always took him a while — he said: with the baker’s boy. You were at the corner.
I said I don’t know what you mean.
And he said: no.
And then he said, after a long pause: good.
That is it. That is the whole thing.

A dying man said eleven words to a twenty-year-old and the twenty-year-old assumed he was confused, because he was on morphine and had been talking about the reeds for two days, and because you were at the corner is not information, it is a fragment.
I did not ask him what he meant. He died two days later.
I have thought about good more than about anything else anybody has ever said to me.
He said no — and then he said good.
He asked me if I knew, I said I did not, and he was relieved.
At the time I did not register it as relief. I registered it as an old man agreeing with me. That is what good sounds like when you have no idea what the question was.
I want to note something about the shape of that memory, because it is the whole of this book.

I did not repress it. I have never forgotten it. I could have told you about it at any point in the last twelve years — I told a colleague about it once, in 2018, as an anecdote about how strange people get at the end.
It sat in the open, completely available, meaning nothing, for twelve years.

That is what a door actually looks like. Not a locked room. A thing on the shelf in the hall that you walk past four thousand times and dust and never once pick up, because there is no reason to, because it is just an object, because nobody has ever told you what it is.
25. THE CALL — the letter that came the other way
She did it in pieces that year, out of order, which is not how she does anything.
She said: I’ll give you a bit.
She said: Afrasiyab wrote to him. Come and see me. Nothing in the letter was wrong. It was warm. It said, we have not seen each other, bring your wife, my daughter, I want to see the child.
She said: and Garsivaz had already been to Siavash and told him the king was turning. And Garsivaz had already been to the king and let him understand that the boy was building something.

She said: so the letter arrived at a young man who had been prepared for two years to read it the wrong way. And he read it the wrong way. And then he behaved as a frightened man behaves, and every single thing he did after that confirmed the story.
She said: that is the technique, Ali. You do not need to make anybody do anything. You just make sure that when they behave normally, it looks like the thing you said.
I said: so he went.
And she said: not yet. He tried to leave first.
She said: he wrote to his father — to Kavus, after everything, after the letter about the hostages, after seven years — and he asked to come home.
There was a pause.
She said: and Kavus said yes.
And she said: and the letter took too long.
I said: that’s —
She said: I know.
She said: that is the cruellest sentence in the poem and it is four words long. The letter took too long. He asked, and he was forgiven, and there was a road between them, and the road had a length.
She said: enough. That’s enough of that.
She said: how’s the knee — no, I’m the one with the knee. How’s your back? You lift things.
26. THE YEARS — the balcony
Amir came in the spring of 2019, which was the second of the two times we saw each other in eleven years.

He was thirty-four and he had a mortgage and a daughter and he had put on the specific fourteen pounds that men from our family put on at that age, and he was still, infuriatingly, the best-looking person in any room he walked into.

He stayed four nights. We did the things. Our father drove up from Irvine for two of them and took us somewhere on Westwood Boulevard that belongs in a different book. We took Amir’s daughter to the aquarium in Long Beach, which neither of us noticed the significance of until my mother pointed it out on the phone afterwards and then we both went quiet.
The third night we were on the balcony at about one in the morning.
He was drinking. I was not, particularly. The lemon tree was doing whatever it does at night.

And we talked about our father for a while, which we can do now, in a way we could not until we were about thirty — the shape of him, in a lawn chair forty miles from where we were sitting, the way he laughed with no sound, the fact that neither of us had managed one real sentence with him in two evenings and both of us were pretending it was the traffic.
And then Amir said, looking out at the street and not at me:
He said: do you ever think about the yard?
I want to describe what happened in my body, because it was not fear.
It was housekeeping.
Something in me went through a set of doors very quickly and quietly, checked that they were shut, and reported back. Two seconds, maybe less. No alarm, no adrenaline, nothing a doctor would find.
And then I said: not really.
And he said: no. Me neither.
And that was it.
He was giving me the door, and he was giving it to me at one in the morning on a balcony with a drink in his hand, which is the only way my brother has ever been able to give anybody anything.

He was not asking me to explain my hands. He has never once asked me about my hands. He was asking whether I still went there, in my head, and he was asking because he was worried about me and had been for fifteen years and did not have any other way to say it.
And I said not really, which was true, which is the terrible part.
I did not lie to my brother on that balcony. I genuinely did not think about the yard. That is what the whole apparatus is for.
He went to bed about twenty minutes later.

And I sat out there for another hour with a lemon tree and thought about nothing much at all, and slept well, and drove him to LAX two days later, and we hugged at the kerb the way we do, badly, twice, and he said ghorboonet beram [ghor-BOO-net be-RAM] — which is a thing our mother says and which means, more or less, may I be sacrificed for you, and which nobody in our family has ever been able to say without making it a joke.
And I drove home on the 105 and that was the closest anybody has ever come.
27. THE YEARS — the addresses
There are, depending on how you count, somewhere between eleven and twenty places in greater Los Angeles where the ten nights are observed.
I know where nine of them are.

I did not seek that out. I want to be clear that at no point did I sit down and research it. It accumulated.
