You live in a city with the largest Iranian population outside Iran and things reach you — a flyer in a grocery on Westwood, a man at a wedding mentioning his heyat in the Valley, a Persian radio station in a taxi in August, a WhatsApp forward from a cousin of Farhad’s that I never opened and never deleted.

By 2019 I could have told you the address of a hall behind a carpet showroom in Northridge, a mosque in Pomona, a house in Encino where about forty men go, and the big one, the one everybody knows, off Sepulveda.
I could have driven to any of them from my apartment in under an hour.
I never went. Not once in eleven years. Not to look, not to stand at the back, not to drive past on the tenth and keep going.
And here is what I want to put down, because it is the strangest fact in this entire book:
I never once decided not to.

There was no decision. There was no evening on which I thought about going and elected not to. There was no year in which I said maybe next year. There was no resistance, because there was nothing to resist — the question never came up.
Eleven Muharrams [mo-har-RAM] went past in a city I lived in, in a country where I was free, at a distance of forty minutes, and the matter simply never arose in my mind at all.
Compare that with what I did do.
I cooked the food. I made gheimeh [ghey-MEH] four or five times a year and got good at it and had people over for it and told them what was in it.

I explained Muharram to Americans. Repeatedly. Well. I have given a version of that explanation perhaps thirty times at dinner tables — the thirst, the river, the tenth day, the reason a thing stays open for thirteen hundred years — and I gave it beautifully, and people were moved by it, and one man in 2018 said it was the most interesting thing he’d heard all year.
I have talked about it more than almost any Iranian I know here.
I have simply never been in the room.

That is not avoidance. Avoidance has a shape and you can feel its edges. I could talk about the tenth day for forty minutes and drive home on the 101 past an exit I knew perfectly well led to a hall where four hundred people were doing it that night, and feel nothing at all, and think about my parking.
I was not hiding from it.
I had it. I owned it. I performed it, competently, for an audience, several times a year.
I had turned the whole of it into material.
28. THE CALL — the one I made
In February 2021 my mother had a small stroke.

She was sixty-two. It happened in the kitchen in the morning and she was on the floor for about forty minutes before Mrs Kazemi came up, and the outcome was as good as those outcomes get — some weakness on the right, some trouble with certain words for about three weeks, and then most of it back.

I found out by text from a cousin because she had told them not to call me until they knew. My father, who was in Irvine that month, rang me twenty minutes after the text, having found out the way he finds out everything about my mother, which is that she had not answered him for a whole morning, and he could not get a sentence out, and rang back an hour later and could.
That is the only time in eleven years I have been genuinely, physically frightened.

I have described a lot of things in this book as though I felt nothing, and it is accurate. That morning I sat on the floor of a bathroom in Frogtown with a phone in my hand and could not stand up for a while.

Everything I had built — the account, the citizenship, the studio, the certificate in a drawer — resolved instantly into one fact, which is that I was eleven thousand kilometres away and there was a flight and I could not take it and get back in, not that year, not with what was happening at the borders, and that if it had gone the other way I would have watched it on a telephone.
The way she watched me graduate.
I called her four days later when she could talk.
And she said, slowly, and I could hear her choosing the words like a woman going up stairs:
She said: I’m all right. Don’t do the voice.
I said what voice.
She said: that one.
And then she said — and this was three weeks in, on a later call, when the words had come back — she said something I have not been able to put down anywhere else.
She said: I was on the floor and I could see under the fridge.
She said: there was a bottle cap under there and I remember thinking, that has been there since Amir was at school.
She said: and then I thought about you, and I thought — and she stopped, and I let her have it — I thought, he’s going to find out from somebody else.
She said: that was the worst part. Not the floor. That.
I said: Maman.
And she said: it’s fine. Mrs Kazemi came.
And then she said, in a completely different voice, the practical one:
She said: I want to finish the story.
I said what?
She said: Siavash. I never finished it. I’ve been not finishing it for two years and we both know it.
She said: I’d like to do it properly. Not tonight.
She said: but I don’t want to leave it like that.
PART FOUR — THE GAZE
29. THE YEARS — Highland Park
I met Reza [re-ZAA] in April 2021 in a garage behind a house in Highland Park that four people were using as a workshop.

I had gone because a woman from the studio was building something and needed a second pair of hands on a Saturday, and there were maybe eight people there, and one of them was nineteen and very tall and very quiet and did not appear to be doing anything.

He was born in Glendale. His parents came in the eighties. He had about forty words of Persian, all of them domestic, and he pronounced his own name the American way and then corrected himself when I said it, which is a thing I have watched a hundred people do here and which never stops being sad.
He asked me what I did and I told him, and he asked a follow-up question that was better than the ones adults ask.
He said: how do you know what to leave out?
I said: you don’t, at first. You put everything in and then you take things away until it starts to hurt, and then you put one thing back.
And he did something that I registered at the time as nothing at all.
He wrote it down.
Not on his phone. On the back of his hand, with a pen off the bench, while I was still talking.
I saw him five or six times over the next two months.

He would turn up where I was. Not in a way that felt like anything — a group thing, an opening, a lunch after a workshop day. Once he came to a talk I gave at a college in Pasadena, forty minutes each way on a bus, and stood at the back and did not ask a question and left before I could say hello.

He started using my sentences. I noticed it the third time. It was not mimicry exactly; it was that a thing I had said about pacing came out of his mouth two weeks later in a slightly better form, and he did not know he was doing it, and I found it enormously flattering and did not examine that for a second.
He asked me what to read. I gave him a list. He read all of it. He came back with the list annotated and disagreed with me about two of them, correctly.
I liked him.
I want that on the record before any of the rest of it, because everything that happened after has made it very hard for me to say that simply.

I liked him. He was nineteen and serious and slightly lost and much cleverer than he had been told, and he had the specific hunger of a kid who has finally met somebody doing the thing he did not know was a thing you could do.
I was thirty-two and I had built a whole life alone and there was a nineteen-year-old writing on his hand while I talked.
Here is what I told myself about it at the time, and I told myself this consciously, in words, more than once:
Somebody did this for me once.
I meant Diane Okafor. Four hundred words on the back of a two-page paper. A woman who remembered my name in the second week.
That is who I thought I was being.
30. THE YEARS — the look
It was the fourth of June 2021, in the same garage, at about nine at night.

We had finished the thing we were doing. There were four of us left and somebody had put beer in a bucket and the roll door was up and it was that specific hour in Los Angeles in June when the day has finally let go and the air is exactly the temperature of a person.
And I was talking.
I do not remember what about. I have tried. It was probably work, because it usually was, and I was probably being good at it, because I usually was.

I know that I did the thing I do, which is to build slowly and hold something back and then give it, and I know that I did it well, because I could feel the small change in the room that tells you it landed. I have been able to feel that since I was fifteen years old. I have never once had to learn it.
And I looked up mid-sentence, the way you do, and Reza was looking at me.
I am going to describe the expression as precisely as I can, and the fact that I can describe it this precisely is the entire problem.
His mouth was slightly open. Not much. Enough that the lower lip had come away.

His head was tilted maybe four or five degrees. Not forward — up, very slightly, which is what a person does when they are looking at something above them, and I was sitting on a stool at the same height as him.
His hands were completely still on his knees. That was the thing. Everybody else in that garage was doing something with their hands. His were dead still, palms down.

And his eyes were not tracking. They were not moving between my eyes and my mouth the way a listener’s eyes move. They were fixed on one point, which I think was the middle of my face, and they were not really looking at me at all. They were looking at something I represented.
And I lost the sentence.

Completely. Mid-clause. I stopped, and somebody laughed and said something, and I said sorry, lost my thread, and picked it up about four words back and finished it, and it was fine, and nobody thought anything of it.
I went out to the car about twenty minutes later.
I sat in the driver’s seat in the dark on a residential street in Highland Park and did not start the engine for a long time.
Because the thing that had happened was not that a young man looked at me admiringly.
The thing that had happened was that I recognised it.
Not understood. Not identified. Recognised, the way you recognise a smell, from the inside, instantly, before language.

I knew that face. I knew the exact tilt of it and the exact stillness of the hands and the exact way the eyes stop tracking, and I knew it with a completeness that you can only have about a face you have made.
I had made that face. Somewhere. At somebody.
And I could not, sitting in that car on the fourth of June 2021, tell you where or when or at whom.
I could tell you the temperature. I could tell you that it was cold and that my hands were cold and that there was a smell of something burning and that I was looking up.
That was all I had. Cold, and up, and burning.
I drove home and made something to eat and went to bed and slept badly for the first time in about nine years.
31. THE YEARS — the body
It came in pieces over the following six weeks and it never once came as a picture.

That is the thing I would most want to explain to somebody who has not had it. Nobody who has this gets a film. There is no scene, no camera, no sequence. What you get is much stupider and much worse than that.
You get temperature. You get texture. You get the specific weight of an object in a hand that is no longer holding it.
The first one was in the shower.

Cold air on wet skin, which is an ordinary thing that happens in a shower, and which arrived that morning attached to something that was not the shower — a certainty, absolutely physical and entirely wordless, that I was outdoors, and that it was extremely early, and that being cold was correct.
I stood in there until the water went and then I stood in there after it went.
The second was gravel.

I was in a parking lot in Glendale and I stepped on some loose grit and my foot did a very small slide, three or four centimetres, the way a foot does, and my whole body reacted as though I had gone off a roof.
Wet gravel. Cold. Under one hand — not both, one, the right one, flat, fingers spread, taking weight.
I had to sit on a wall.
The third one is the one that frightened me, and it came in my own kitchen while I was cooking, and it was in my hands.

Weight. A specific mass in the right hand, hanging down, about the weight of a full bottle of water, distributed wrong — heavier at the bottom, with give in it, the way a bundle of loose things is heavy.

And an absolute conviction, arriving with the weight and inseparable from it, that this object was mine. That it had been given to me. That somebody had put it in my hand and told me it was mine and that I had believed him completely.
I put down what I was holding and looked at my hand and there was nothing in it and there had been nothing in it for eighteen years.
By the middle of July I had, in total:

Cold. Early. Outdoors. Wet gravel under the right palm. A weight in the right hand that was mine. A smell of something burning that was not wood and not food. A sound, once, that I could not identify and that made me put both hands flat on a table.
And up. Always up. Whatever I was doing in that memory, I was looking up at something.
That is what people mean when they say the body keeps the score, and it is a phrase I had heard perhaps forty times in this country and had always understood as a metaphor.
It is not a metaphor. It is a filing problem.

The score is kept in a place that does not do sentences. It does temperature and load and angle and smell, because those are the things the animal needs, and it will hand them back to you in a parking lot in Glendale eighteen years later with no context whatsoever and no explanation and no order, and it will not tell you what they are for, because it does not know. It only knows they mattered.
32. THE YEARS — I held
I want to be very careful in this chapter, because it is where a different book would have its collapse, and I did not have one.
I did not fall apart in the summer of 2021.

I want to say that plainly and I want the reader to sit with how unsatisfying it is. There was no breakdown. I did not miss work. I did not drink. I did not call anybody at three in the morning. I did not go to a doctor and I did not, at any point, tell one single human being that anything was happening.
I held.
Here is what holding actually consists of, in case anybody thinks it is passive.
It is work. It is a set of learned techniques, applied deliberately, several times a day, by a competent adult who is good at things.

You get up at the same time. You do not lie in the bed after the alarm, because that is where it comes. You put something on immediately — talk, not music, because talk occupies the language part and music does not. You make the day structurally full, front to back, with tasks that require your hands and your judgement, because a task that only requires your hands leaves you free and free is the enemy. You do not sit in a parked car. You do not stand in the shower. You do not, under any circumstances, allow yourself to be tired and warm and horizontal and unoccupied at the same time.
And when it comes anyway, in the middle of something, you do the thing I do not know how to describe except physically:

You put your attention on an object in the room and you make it the only object. A door handle. The grain in a bench. You describe it to yourself in sentences. You keep describing it until the sentences take over, because the thing in your chest does not have sentences and cannot follow you into them.
Then you carry on with what you were doing.
I had all of that. Fully assembled, tested, reliable, and I had built it myself with no help from anybody, and here is the thing:
I did not build it that summer.

I had had it for years. Decades, possibly. I did not invent a single one of those techniques in 2021 — I already had them, the way you already have a way of walking. I had been holding something for eighteen years with a set of tools so well worn that I had stopped experiencing them as tools and had begun experiencing them as my personality.
I like to get up early. I don’t like sitting around. I’m not a lie-in person. I like to be busy. I’m not really an introspective guy.
Every one of those is true. Every one of those is a thing my friends would say about me, affectionately, correctly.
Every one of those is a hand on a door.
And it worked.

That is the part I need people to hear. It worked. Six weeks of the worst thing that had ever happened to my body and nobody in my life noticed, and my work did not suffer, and I was, by every external measure and most internal ones, fine.
I am not describing a failure. I am describing a success.

I was extremely good at this. I had been made extremely good at this by eleven years of behaving as though I was alone in a country where nobody could help me and nothing was coming, and every single quality that got me from a car wash on Sepulveda to a life I built with my own hands was, that summer, deployed at full strength, with total competence, against myself.
The strength is the lock. There is no other lock. There never was.
33. THE YEARS — the angle
The thing that broke it was not a memory. It was a measurement.
I want to be exact about this because it is the most useful thing I have to offer anybody who has one of these, and it is not what people expect.
It was arithmetic.
For eighteen years I had a thing I had always understood as the central event of my adolescence, and I had always understood it as a gift, and it had a very specific and unvarying shape:
I was above.

That is what it was. That is the whole phenomenon. Every tenth night, from the age of nine, I left my body and looked down at a yard from a point about four metres above the tarpaulin, and I could see the crowd and the bulbs and the tear in the corner that nobody fixed, and I saw everything from above.

And in the last year I ever did it, it moved. It went sideways over the wall, over the shop roof, over the main road, three streets, and it stopped over an alley. And I looked down into that alley and saw a man on the ground and men standing round him.
Down. Always down. Everything I have ever told anybody about this, including in a book, is a description of looking down.

And in the last week of July 2021 I was doing something completely unrelated — I was working out sightlines for a room, which is my actual job, which is literally a job about where a person’s eyes are — and I had a plan on a screen and I was standing an imaginary human being at an imaginary door.
And a thing arrived in my chest with no warning at all and no words attached and I had to put both hands on the desk.
Because everything my body had given me that summer was level.
Cold air on the face. Not on the top of the head. On the face, straight on.
Gravel under the right palm, flat, taking weight — which means I was down on one hand, which means I was on the ground, which means I was in a body, which means I had one.
A weight in the right hand, hanging down at the end of an arm.
And up. Always up. Six weeks of fragments and every single one of them was looking up.
You do not look up from four metres above a tarpaulin. There is nothing up there. There is sky.
I sat down at my own desk in Frogtown at about four in the afternoon on a Tuesday and did the geometry with a pencil like a schoolboy.

If I am at eye level. If I am four metres away. If the ground slopes toward a drain and the man’s head is at the low end and I am at the high end at the mouth of it. If there is a bulb in a wire cage above a green gate and it is above me and to my left, which is why I am looking up, which is why my face is cold, which is why there is a smell of something burning that is not wood.
Then everything fits. All of it. Every fragment, in one position, with nothing left over.
I was standing at the mouth of the alley.
I would like to describe what I felt and I cannot, because I did not feel anything for about ninety seconds. I have been told this is common. There is a gap.
What I did was: I closed the file, I saved it, I said goodnight to two people, I drove home on Riverside with the radio off, I parked, and I sat in the car outside my own building for four hours.
And at some point in that four hours the last piece went in, and it went in quietly, the way the worst ones do.
Because if I was standing at the mouth of that alley at four in the morning on Ashura [aa-shoo-RAA] when I was fourteen years old — then somebody in that alley could see me.
34. THE CALL — the basin
She rang on a Sunday in August, in the morning her time, and she said: are you free? and I said yes.
And she said: I’m going to finish it.
She said: he went.
Farangis told him not to. She was seven months pregnant and she was the king’s own daughter and she knew that court better than anybody alive and she said: whatever the letter says, do not go.
And he went, because he had a system, and the system was that if you stand in front of people and you are innocent, it comes out all right.
She said: they arrested him on the road.
She said: Garsivaz had gone ahead of him. Of course he had. He had ridden ahead and told his brother that Siavash was coming with an army, which was three hundred men and a pregnant wife.

She said: and Afrasiyab came out and saw him and — and this is the detail I have never got over, Ali — for a moment it nearly did not happen. He saw the boy’s face and something moved in him. Ferdowsi says it. He looked at him and hesitated.
She said: and then Garsivaz said something. One more small thing. And that was the end of it.
She said: they took him out to open ground.

She said: and Farangis got out of wherever they had put her and came and threw herself in front of her father and pulled her own hair out. That is in the poem. She tore her hair and clawed her face and said, he came to you, he had nowhere else, my mother’s God will not forgive you.
She said: and Afrasiyab had her taken away and locked up.
There was a pause on the line and I said nothing at all.
She said: now I want you to hear how they did it, because it is the whole poem.
She said: they did not kill him where he stood.
They dragged him some distance out. And they had brought a basin.
And they held him over it.
She said: and Ali — this is the thing — they did it that way so that his blood would not touch the ground.
I said: why?
And my mother, from a kitchen in Elahieh, with a bad right hand, said:
Because they knew what innocent blood does when it touches the ground. It cries out. It makes something grow. It brings the thing back.

She said: they were not being tidy, my love. They were being careful. They were frightened of what he would become if any of it got out, and so they held a young man over a bowl and made sure the earth did not get a single drop.
She said: and one drop got out anyway.
She said: one. That is all that ever gets out.

And where it fell, a plant came up. It came up the same day, out of nothing, out of hard ground, and it had leaves like a hand, and it is still called what it is called: par-e siavashan [PAR-e see-yaa-vaa-SHAAN]. Siavash’s feather.
She said: you know it. You have seen it a thousand times. It grows on the wet stone at the edge of every fountain in this country. It’s the little fern.
She said: you can buy it in a pot on Vali Asr.
I did not say anything for so long that she said: Ali jan.
And I said: I’m here.
And she said: it’s all right. It’s a very old story.
And I said: Maman —
And she said: yes?
And I did not do it.

I had it in my mouth. I was thirty-three years old sitting on the floor of my own kitchen in Los Angeles with the phone on the tiles beside me and my mother was there, awake, willing, in the room where I learned to read, and I had it in my mouth.
And I said: nothing. I said, it’s a good story.
And she said: it’s not a good story. It’s a true one.
She said: they’re different.
35. THE YEARS — the gate
Here is what I know and here is how I know it, and I want the difference between those two things to be visible on the page, because I have spent two years trying to keep it visible in my own head.
What I know.

On the tenth day of Muharram, in the winter I was fourteen, I got up before four in the morning and left my uncle’s flat in Nazi Abad [naa-ZEE aa-BAAD] and walked three streets and stood at the mouth of an alley a metre and a half wide with a bulb in a wire cage over a green gate, and I watched what was happening in that yard.
I do not have a memory of doing it. I have a body that will not stop describing it.
How I know.

Cold on the face and not the crown, which means level. Right palm on wet gravel, which means down on one hand, which means I had a body. A weight in the right hand which was mine, which was a chain, which Agha Sadegh had given me every year since I was nine and which I had carried through the streets that night with the rest of them. Looking up, which means the bulb. Burning, which is naphtha, which is what they used in that neighbourhood to get a brazier going before dawn in Esfand. And the geometry, which fits at one position and no other.
And: you were at the corner. Eleven words from a dying man in 1387 that I have carried for twelve years and understood as morphine.

And: my grandfather stood me at that corner when I was six and nobody ever told me, and I inherited a habit I have no memory of having and walked to a gate I had never been to and knew which one it was.
That is the case. It is entirely circumstantial. There is no photograph, there is no witness who has spoken, and there is no living person who has told me a single word of it.

I want that on the record because a great deal follows from it and I am aware — I am extremely aware — that I am a man who is very good at building something out of pieces and making people believe it.
That is literally my job. I put fragments in a room in an order and a stranger walks out convinced.
But there is one more thing and it is not circumstantial, and it is the reason I stopped arguing with myself in August 2021.
For six years, every tenth night, I put myself four metres in the air.
Not once. Every time. For six consecutive years, in a state I did not control and had never chosen, the single unvarying feature was that I was above the yard, looking down.
There is only one thing on earth that a fourteen-year-old boy is doing when he removes himself from his own body every single time and hangs above it, and it is not receiving a gift.
He is getting out of a position.
I was not being shown anything. I was being taken somewhere else.
And the one place I was never, in six years, in any state, at any tempo, allowed to be — was standing at eye level, four metres away, at the mouth of that alley, with a chain in my right hand.
36. THE YEARS — he saw me
This is the shortest chapter in this book and I have rewritten it eleven times.
If I was standing at the mouth of that alley, then Sohrab Ayeneh [soh-RAAB aa-yee-NEH] looked up and saw a fourteen-year-old boy in the gateway.

He knew me. He had covered a microphone once so that two hundred men would make a corridor for me and my tray. He knew whose grandson I was. He knew I had his part in the play the following year, or would have, or was about to.
And he was twenty-four, and he was in the middle of it, and he was being watched.
I have run every other version. I want that understood. I have spent two years running every other version, professionally, the way I would interrogate a room I was building.

That he did not see me. That he saw me and it changed nothing. That the cut was already made. That a scalp artery is a scalp artery and men have died of it who nobody was watching. That my uncle said wait and eleven minutes passed and none of that has anything to do with a boy in a gateway.
All of those are possible. Several of them are likely. I cannot disprove one of them.
And I know what I know, which is what happens to a person when they are being looked at.

I know it because I have had it my entire life. I have had a yard of four hundred men look at me and I have felt what it does. I have stood in front of a room and felt the moment it lands and gone one step further than I was going to go. I did it in a garage in Highland Park on the fourth of June and lost my sentence when the boy’s hands went still.
Being looked at makes people go further. That is all it does. That is its entire function.

And on the tenth day of Muharram, in a yard behind a green gate, before it was light, a man who could hear a room was in the middle of the only thing he ever did that nobody was allowed to watch — and a child he loved was standing in the gateway with his mouth open, looking up.
I do not know that it was because of me.

I know that I was there, and that I have spent eighteen years hanging four metres above a tarpaulin rather than be there, and that when the thing finally came back it came back as cold and up and a weight in my right hand.

And I know that of everything my body handed me over six weeks in the summer of 2021, the piece it would not give me — the only one, the piece I do not have and have never had and am now certain I will never get — is his face.
PART FIVE — THE EVENING
37. THE CALL — the morning of
She rang at seven in the morning my time, which was half past six in the evening there, on Thursday the nineteenth of August 2021.
She had no reason. She had stopped bothering with reasons that year.
She said: are you working today?
I said I was.
She said: what is it? The one with the water, or the other one?

And I told her about it — a small permanent room at a water authority out in the east of the county, about where the water comes from and what it costs and who fought about it in 1913 — and she listened to all of it, the whole way through, the way she has listened to me describe things since I was four.
And at the end she said: that’s a good one. That’s the sort you’re good at. You’ll want to make them stand still first.
Which is exactly what I had done, and which I had not told her, and I said: that’s what I did.
And she said: well. I’m not stupid.
She said: your grandmother does not understand a single thing about your life. Either of them.
I said: no.
She said: they want you married and closer. They were horrible about the hair.
And then she said, and it was completely unweighted, the way she puts the enormous things down:
She said: I understand it. I want you to know I understand all of it.

She said: I know what you did. I know what it cost. You went to a country where you had nobody who was obliged to you, at twenty-one, with two bad hands and you built the whole thing yourself and nobody helped you and I have never once had to worry about whether you would manage.
She said: most mothers do not get that. Most of us worry until we die.
She said: I have not worried about whether you would manage since about 2013.
I said: Maman.
And she said: what.
And I said: nothing. It’s early.
She said: it’s always early there. It’s a stupid country.
Then she said: what are you doing tonight?
And I said — and this is completely true, and I had not planned it, and I had not thought about it once until the words were out of my mouth:
I said: I don’t know. Nothing.
And she said: good. Do nothing. You never do nothing.
38. THE YEARS — an ordinary reason
Somebody at work said it at about four in the afternoon.

That is all. A woman called Nasrin, who is fifty and from here since she was six and who I have never once discussed anything with beyond work, was on the phone to her mother in the corridor and I heard about nine words of it and one of them was shaam-e ghariban [shaam-eh gha-ree-BAAN].
And I stood there with a coffee and thought: is it already?
I looked it up on my phone at my desk like a foreigner. That is what I want on the record. I checked the date of Ashura on a website, in English, the way you would check when Diwali is.
The nineteenth. Tonight.
I want to be accurate about my state of mind at four o’clock on that afternoon, because everything after this is going to look like a decision and it was not one.

I was not resolved. I had not been building toward it. I had spent six weeks working out where I had been standing when I was fourteen and had told nobody and had held, successfully, and had every intention of continuing to hold, and I had no plan of any kind that involved a hall or a night or two hundred strangers.
What happened was much smaller and much stupider.
I thought: it’s August.
I had never once, in my entire life, been in a Muharram that was not in the cold.

The early ones were spring, the tail of winter, snow still on the mountains. The last ones, the ones that count, were Esfand. Minus four or five. Breath going up under the bulbs. My whole body knows the month as a temperature, and the temperature is cold.
And I was standing in an office in Los Angeles in a T-shirt and it was ninety-four degrees outside and the asphalt in the lot was soft.

The calendar had walked. Eleven days a year, for eighteen years, which is about two hundred days, which is most of a season and a bit, and it had carried the tenth of Muharram out of the snow and into high summer without asking anybody.
The tenth day is about thirst.
And in Tehran I had spent six years mourning it in a coat.
That is why I went. I want to be honest even though it is unimpressive.
Not to confront anything. Not to remember. Not to grieve.
I went because I wanted to know what it was like in the heat.
I drove out of Frogtown at about half past six with the sun still fully up and the freeway the colour of a coin, and I did not put anything on in the car.
39. THE YEARS — the man with the dish
It was a rented hall behind a business on a boulevard and the lot was full so I parked two streets down and walked.

Ninety-four degrees at seven in the evening. The asphalt gave slightly under my shoe at the edge where it meets the kerb, the way it does out here in August, and I registered that and did not think about why I registered it.

Black banners on the fence with the white writing. Same writing. A folding sign on the pavement in Persian and English. Minivans. Children running in the lot in good clothes, at speed, weaving between cars in the way children do at these things everywhere on earth.
There was an ice chest by the door with bottles of water in it and a boy of about nine standing next to it whose entire job was to make sure it stayed full.
I stood on the far side of the lot for I do not know how long.
There was a folding table by the door with a stack of foam containers on it and a man behind it.
He was about sixty and he was wearing a good coat.

That is the first thing I noticed, because it was ninety-four degrees and he was in a coat, and he was in a coat because it was the tenth and you wear a coat. I have known men like that my whole life and I had not seen one for eleven years.
Grey at the temples. Glasses pushed up on his head and forgotten about. Not a religious-looking man at all — a man who had come from somewhere else, an accountant, a dentist, a man with an office.
And his hands were wrong for the coat. Thick across the back. One thumbnail gone black. The fingers of a man who did something with them for thirty years before he did whatever he does now.
He was not looking at anybody.
He was doing the thing men do at that table, which is lift the lid, ladle, close it, hand it over, take the next, and he did not stop while people spoke to him.
I knew that rhythm. I had seen it from underneath, at the height of a tea tray, in another country, from a man with forearms like a door.
I did not decide to walk over. My legs did it while I was still on the other side of the lot thinking about the coat.
He put a container in my hands without looking up.

It was warm through the bottom and I had to change hands, and I looked at it and it was gheimeh. Split peas, dried lime, meat cooked down to nothing. A spoon of rice with saffron dragged across the top the way somebody’s mother taught somebody.
In a foam container with the lid steaming on the inside, in a parking lot, on a boulevard, at ninety-four degrees.
And he said the thing. Not a greeting. The sentence that goes with the object and no other sentence, flat, already looking past me at the next person:
Ghabool bashe. God accept it.
And I said the answer.

I did not decide to. I had not said it in eleven years and my mouth had it, whole, in the right register, in the accent of a neighbourhood eleven thousand kilometres away that I have not lived in since I was fifteen.
And the man’s eyes came back up.

Because it is not the words. Anybody can learn the words. It was the south of it, in a parking lot on a boulevard, out of a man in his thirties in a linen shirt who had come from somewhere with money.
He looked at me for slightly too long.
Then he said: bokhor, pesaram.
Eat, my son.
And he put the ladle back in the pot and took the next container off the stack.
The whole thing was thirty seconds. I never learned his name. I have never seen him again and I have looked.
I stood at the edge of that lot with a warm foam container in both hands and could not have told you what was happening to me.
Here is what was happening to me.

I had been in this country eleven years and I had built every single thing in my life with my own two ruined hands and I had been extremely proud of that, and it had made me strong, and the strength was the lock.
And a man in a coat in a parking lot handed me a hot meal I had not earned, had not applied for, had not achieved, and could not refuse.

That is what that food is. That is the entire mechanism and I had explained it beautifully at about thirty dinner tables in this country. You may not sell it. You may not keep the good part. You may not ask who is taking it. And the man taking it is not accepting charity — he is helping somebody pay a debt they owe.
He was doing me the favour.
I ate about half of it standing up, next to a fence, in the heat, like a man at a bus stop.
Then I put it in a bin and wiped my hands on my jeans and went in.
40. THE YEARS — the room
I got about a metre and a half inside the door and my feet stopped, and it took me a second to understand why, and the reason was that I already knew where everything was.
Not the room. I had never been in that room. It was a rented hall in Los Angeles with a drop ceiling and a fire exit sign and a laminate floor that somebody had put rugs over.
But the arrangement.
The shoes were to the left inside the door, in a heap, on a piece of plastic sheeting. Of course they were. Where else would they be.
The tea was at the back on the right, on two trestle tables, with the glasses upside down on a cloth and a boy of about eleven in charge of it who did not want to be.

The old men were on chairs along the wall, on the left, near the front — not at the back where the chairs would be more comfortable, at the front, on the hard ones, because that is where they have sat since they were fifty.
The curtain was up the middle, and behind it the women’s side, and the sound coming from behind it was slightly different in a way I could not have described and could identify instantly.
And the front — the strip of carpet in front of the microphone, two metres deep, empty — was empty because it is always empty, because that is where the men go when it starts.

I have been in perhaps four thousand rooms since I was fifteen. I have designed sixty of them professionally. My entire trade is knowing where a person’s body will go in a space they have never been in before.
And I stood in the door of a rented hall in a country I had lived in for eleven years and my feet knew the floor plan of a yard in Nazi Abad.

I went to the back and sat down against the wall with my knees up, which is where I have always sat when I have not been at the front, and it was only about ten minutes later that I understood that I had not sat like that since 2004.
There were maybe two hundred and thirty people. Half of them under forty.

There were boys in basketball shorts. There were two girls behind the curtain-edge on their phones, unbothered, being told by somebody to put them away. There was a man in front of me in a Dodgers cap that he took off when the cleric started and put back on afterwards without thinking about it.
Somebody’s grandmother had brought a folding stool from home.
Half the conversation in that room was in English.
And I want to put this down because I had not expected it and it undid something in me before anything had even started.
It was cheerful.

Before it begins, that room is a party. People had not seen each other since last year. Men were embracing each other and asking after businesses. Somebody was being congratulated about a daughter. Two men were arguing about parking with enormous energy. A woman was going along the row with a plate of dates and would not take no.

I had forgotten that. Eighteen years and I had somehow kept only the last four hours of every night and thrown away the first two, and the first two are this, and the first two are the reason anybody comes.
I sat against a wall in a room full of strangers being pleased to see each other and I thought, with no warning at all and no particular emotion:
I have not been in a room like this since I was fifteen years old.
And then a man I had never seen went up to the microphone and tapped it twice with his finger and the whole room began to sit down.
41. THE YEARS — the telling
The cleric spoke for about thirty-five minutes and it was boring and it was supposed to be.

He talked about debt, and about being decent to people who work for you, and he made two jokes that landed and one that did not. He had an accent from Isfahan [es-fa-HAAN] and about a fifth of what he said was in English for the room, which he did without any apparent feeling about it.
It is flat ground. That is what that part is. You stand on it before the ground tilts.

I sat against the wall with my knees up and let it go past me and thought about nothing at all, and about halfway through I noticed that I was comfortable, and it was the first time I had been comfortable in six weeks.
Then the man who was doing the rowzeh came up. Fifties, ordinary suit, a folder.
And he did what they do, which is start somewhere absurdly small.
He did not start with the battle. He did not start with the river or the army or the tenth day.
He started with a woman making bread.

He said: think about the last normal morning in that camp. The sixth of the month. Nobody has been cut off from the water yet. Somebody is making bread. There are fifty-odd children in those tents and somebody has to feed them and it is an ordinary Tuesday and somebody is kneading dough with sand in it because you cannot keep sand out of anything in that country.
And he stayed there. He stayed in that tent, on that morning, with a woman and some dough, for about six minutes.
I want to describe what he was doing, because I do it for a living and I have never once seen it done better by anybody.
He was making you stand still.

He would not let you have the tenth day. He would not let you have the thing you came for. He held you in a tent on an ordinary morning until you had a woman’s hands in your head, and only then — only when the room had somebody to lose — did he let the seventh of the month happen.
That is the whole craft. Give them somebody alive for four minutes. Then the second wall.
I built a room in a county historical society in 2016 on exactly that principle and won a small award for it and told a woman I admired that I did not know where I had learned it.

And he was good. He was really good. He was not as good as the man I grew up with, and I knew that within ninety seconds, and I want to note that I made that judgement instantly and professionally and without any feeling whatsoever, the way you would notice a joint that was not quite square.
And then he got to the seventh, and the water, and the three days, and the children going quiet — and I felt something happen in my chest and it was not what I had spent six weeks bracing for.
It was fondness.

I sat against the wall in a rented hall in Los Angeles and thought about a boy of eleven carrying a tray of tea at chin height through a standing crowd, in the dark, with his forearms shaking, being the only person in the building allowed to move.
And I smiled. Actually smiled, in a room where two hundred people were beginning to weep.
I had not thought about the tray in eighteen years.
42. THE YEARS — my mouth had it
The nowheh started and I knew the words.
I want to be precise about the sequence, because it took about four seconds and it is the whole of this chapter.
The lead voice sang the first line. And before he had finished it, before I had recognised the thing or placed it or done anything at all with my mind, my mouth had already begun the response.
Not out loud. My lips moved. Some air came out.

Eighteen years. I had not thought of that line, sought it out, heard it, or been near it in eighteen years. If you had put a pen in my hand that afternoon and offered me money to write down one line of one nowheh I would have handed you a blank sheet.
And a stranger sang four words and something below language answered him.
I sat there with my hand over my mouth like a man who has hiccuped in a lecture.
Then the slow section. The latmiyeh [lat-mee-YEH].

Open hand on the chest, once about every second and a half. Two hundred people. And the sound of it is not what you think, it is not a clap and it is not a drum, it is wet, and it arrives from every direction at once, and you feel it in your own sternum before you have decided anything.
And I did not join in. I want that on the record. I sat against a wall with my knees up and my hands on the floor and I did not lift a hand.

And my chest went anyway. Half a beat behind, the way a foot taps. I could feel it doing it. I put a hand flat on my own sternum like a man checking for a heartbeat and it was going with them and I had not authorised it.
And this is where it came, and it did not come as horror.
It came as pleasure.

I am fifteen years old and I am at the front, three metres from the shop door, and it is minus four and there is fine dry snow going sideways under the bulbs and my back is opened up and my throat is gone.
And it is the best feeling I have ever had in my life.
I need to be extremely clear here because this is the sentence I have been avoiding for forty chapters.
Nothing in America has come near it.

Not the degree. Not the certificate in the drawer. Not the first room with my name on it, or the woman who taught me telling me I had built it like a piece of music, or the morning I got citizenship, or standing in the ocean up to my knees every October, or my mother on a telephone at four in the morning saying she had seen me in a stadium.
All of that was good. Some of it was better than good. I built it out of nothing and I earned every gram of it and I would not give one hour of it back.
And none of it has ever come within a hundred miles of what I felt at fifteen years old, in the cold, at the front, on the tenth night.

That is the thing nobody will let you say. Everybody wants the yard to have been the wound. The yard was the wound. The yard was also the only time in my life I have been entirely inside my own experience with four hundred people breathing at my speed, and the fact that a man was running it at a hundred and twenty-nine beats a minute for money does not make one single second of what I felt untrue.
Both. It was both. It has always been both and it will be both until I die.
And I sat against that wall in Los Angeles at ninety-four degrees and I began to cry, quietly, with my hand over my mouth, and nobody looked at me, because that is what the room is for.
43. THE YEARS — the shoor
The lead voice lifted and the beat doubled and the shoor [SHOOR] came in.
Two hundred people stood up. The Dodgers cap came off. The boys in basketball shorts went forward into the empty two metres of carpet without being told, the way you go, because you have always gone.

And the sound went up in that hall the way it goes up, and the second voice came in on the delay, saying the name, over and over, into the machine, so that it came back doubled and stacked and became the clock.
And I estimated the tempo.

I did not decide to. I have done it in cars and gyms and supermarkets for nine years and called it a preference, and I did it in a rented hall on the nineteenth of August 2021 and got a number, and the number was in the window.

It was not his number. I want to say that. It was somewhere in the region and it was not exact and the man on the microphone was thirty-something and from Encino and had never heard of a butcher in Nazi Abad.
That is just how fast this is done.

That is what I finally understood standing at the back of that hall. Nobody designed the window for me. It is where the human body goes. He did not invent it — he found it, in me, the way you find a note in a room by clapping.
And then I went.
Not out of my body. That never came back and it is never coming back and I have stopped waiting for it.
Something much simpler and much more embarrassing.
I was happy.

Whole-body, chest open, weeping, standing at the back of a rented hall behind a business on a boulevard in the San Fernando Valley at ninety-four degrees with two hundred strangers, and it was good, and it was the thing I had been missing every single day since the eighteenth of May 2010 and had never once, in eleven years, allowed myself to name.
I have been happy in this country. I said so and I meant it.
This was different and it was not better and it was not worse and there is no scale that has both of them on it.
And in the middle of it — in the absolute middle, at the top of it, with my eyes shut and my chest going and my face wet — the angle changed.
There was no picture. There was never going to be a picture.
My body simply supplied the correct viewing position, the way it had been trying to for six weeks, and this time it did not send a fragment. It sent the whole arrangement at once.

Eye level. Four metres. Cold on the face, not the crown. Right palm down on wet gravel. A weight in the right hand that was mine. A bulb in a wire cage, above and to the left, which is why I am looking up.
A green gate.
And a man in the middle of a small yard, in the middle of the only thing he ever did that nobody was allowed to watch.
Looking back at me.
And I held.
That is what happened. That is all that happened.
I did not go down. I did not make a sound. I did not leave the room.

I did what I have done ten thousand times, what I have been better at than almost anybody I have ever met, what eleven years of doing it alone in a foreign country built in me and what a car wash on Sepulveda started:
I put my attention on an object.

There was a fire exit sign above the door on the far wall, green and white, with a running man on it and an arrow. I looked at the running man. I described him to myself in sentences. I described the arrow. I described the little bracket the sign was mounted on and the two screws in the bracket and the fact that one of them was a different colour from the other.
And the sentences took over, because the thing in my chest does not have sentences and cannot follow me into them.
And the door shut.
It took, I would estimate, eleven seconds.
I stood at the back of that hall for another forty minutes and my face dried and I was completely fine.
44. THE YEARS — the chairs
It ended the way it ends, which is that it does not end so much as thin out.

The shoor stops. Somebody says something into the microphone about next year and about a man who is in hospital and would people please remember him. The lights, which have been half off, come all the way on, and everybody looks worse, and everybody starts talking at once.
Then the chairs.
I do not know why I stayed.

I have thought about that more than anything else in this chapter. The lot was emptying. I had a car two streets down. I had held, successfully, and I was fine, and every instinct I have built over eighteen years was telling me to go home and have a glass of water and get up at the same time tomorrow.
I stayed. I stood at the back with my hands in my pockets while two hundred people put their shoes on.
The man stacking the chairs was about my age.
He was in a black shirt with the sleeves pushed up and he was doing it efficiently and alone, six at a time, walking them to a trolley by the fire exit. Nobody had asked him to. He was one of those.
I do not know his name. I did not ask. He did not offer.
He came past me with a stack and stopped and looked at me for a second and said:
You all right, boss?
Completely ordinary. American. Slightly Valley. A man clearing a room, being polite to the last person in it.
And I told him a story.
I want to describe what I did, exactly, because it is the last thing that happens in this book and because I have spent two years unable to decide what it was.
I said: sorry. First one in eleven years.
And he put the chairs down.

And I told him about a yard behind a butcher’s shop in south Tehran, and about being nine years old and not speaking for six weeks, and about a man with forearms like a door who put me at the front because he did not know what else to do with a child who would not talk, and about an old man who gave me a chain out of a trunk every year and always the same one.

I told him about the cold. About the tarpaulin and the tear in the corner nobody fixed in six years. About the smell of the pots at three in the morning. About a boy carrying tea at chin height through a crowd of men who moved for him without looking.
I told him about a voice that could sit on a low note four times and refuse to give you the high one until four hundred men were leaning forward like wheat.
And I told him — because it was the version I had — that the man with that voice went to Dubai.
It took about four minutes.
And it was magnificent.
That is the thing. That is the whole thing and I need to put it down plainly.
It was the best four minutes of storytelling I have ever done in my life. Better than any room I have built. Better than anything I have said at any table in this country in eleven years.

I gave him the tea tray first. I gave him a person alive, for a minute and a half, before I gave him anything that hurt. I put the cold in early so he could feel it, and I held the chain back until the third thing, and I did not tell him what happened to my hands because I have known since I was fifteen years old that you do not give them the high note when they are leaning.

Every single technique I used on that man in that hall, I took from a dead man in a yard eleven thousand kilometres away, and I have been using them professionally for six years, and I did not choose one of them consciously.
I have never once been more myself than I was in those four minutes.
And I do not know what I was doing.

I have run every version. That I was finally telling somebody, at thirty-three, after eighteen years, and that it happened to come out well because I am good at things. That I was performing. That there is no difference. That a man who tells the truth beautifully is still telling the truth. That a man who has just shut a door in his own chest and then immediately talks for four minutes about the room the door is in has not opened anything at all — he has given a tour of the outside of the building.
I told him everything except the alley, the gate, the eleven minutes, and Sohrab’s name.
I told him everything except the thing.
I have not been able to work out, in two years, whether that was because I could not, or because it is a better story without it.
He did not say anything for a moment.
And then he did the thing.

His mouth came slightly open. His head went up four or five degrees, though we were the same height. His hands, which had been moving the entire time I had been in that hall, went completely still on the top chair of the stack.
And his eyes stopped tracking.
I have seen that face twice in my life and made it once.
He said: man.
He said: you should write that down.

And I stood in an emptying hall in the San Fernando Valley on the nineteenth of August 2021, at thirty-three years old, in a country I chose, having built everything I have out of nothing with two hands that do not close, with a stranger looking at me the way I once looked at somebody, and I understood — with no feeling at all, the way you understand the weather — exactly what I am, and exactly what I am good at, and exactly what it costs, and exactly who paid.
And he said: seriously, though. You all right?
And I said:
Yes.
And I meant it, and I have not stopped meaning it, and I have not stopped hearing myself say it.
GLOSSARY

Persian and Arabic terms and figures appearing in this book. Phonetics are given as plain English syllables, with the stressed syllable in capitals. advieh [ad-vee-YEH] — Persian, spices. A household blend, varying by family, sent between them.
Afrasiyab [af-raa-see-YAAB] — king of Turan, Iran’s ancient enemy; the man who took Siavash in.
Ashura [aa-shoo-RAA] — Arabic, from ’ashara, ten. The tenth day of
Muharram.
Elahieh [e-laa-hee-YEH] — an affluent district in the north of Tehran.
Esfand [es-FAND] — the last month of the Iranian solar year; late winter.
Farangis [fa-raan-GEES] — daughter of Afrasiyab; wife of Siavash.
One of the few women in the Shahnameh permitted to be right and not listened to.
Ferdowsi [fer-dow-SEE] — the poet who compiled the Shahnameh,
The Book of Kings, around the year 1000.
Garsivaz [gar-see-VAAZ] — brother of Afrasiyab. He never lied; he chose what to mention.
ghabool bashe [gha-BOOL baa-SHEH] — may it be accepted. What is said when votive food is handed over.
gharib [gha-REEB] — Arabic, stranger. Not someone unknown, but someone far from their own people and therefore unprotected — a person with nobody obliged to come. Plural Ghariban
[gha-ree-BAAN].
gheimeh [ghey-MEH] — a stew of split peas, meat and dried lime, cooked in bulk and given away during Muharram.
ghorboonet beram [ghor-BOO-net be-RAM] — literally may I be sacrificed for you. An ordinary endearment.
heyat [hey-AT] — Arabic, a body, a form. A neighbourhood mourning association.
Isfahan [es-fa-HAAN] — a city in central Iran, and an accent.
Karaj [ka-RAJ] — a city west of Tehran.
Kavus [kaa-VOOS] — king of Iran; father of Siavash. He knew his wife was lying and let his son ride into the fire anyway.
Khordad [khor-DAAD] — the third month of the Iranian year; late spring.
latmiyeh [lat-mee-YEH] — Arabic, from latm, to strike. The slow chest-beating section of a mourning night.
Mordad [mor-DAAD] — the fifth month; high summer.
Muharram [mo-har-RAM] — Arabic, forbidden. The first month of the
Islamic year, in which Hossein was killed at Karbala. Because the lunar year runs short, it moves backwards through the seasons and takes about thirty-three years to return.
Nazi Abad [naa-ZEE aa-BAAD] — a working-class district in the south of Tehran.
nowheh [now-HEH] — Arabic, from nawh, wailing; the cry of a dove.
The sung lament, performed in call and response.

par-e siavashan [PAR-e see-yaa-vaa-SHAAN] — Siavash’s feather. The maidenhair fern, said to have grown where one drop of his blood escaped the basin. It grows on wet stone at the edge of fountains throughout Iran.
Rostam [ros-TAM] — the great hero of the Shahnameh. He raised
Siavash and taught him everything, and then handed him back.
rowzeh [row-ZEH] — Persian, garden. The prose telling of the Karbala story, from a book written in 1502 whose title became the word for the telling itself.

shaam-e ghariban [shaam-eh gha-ree-BAAN] — the evening of the strangers. The night after Ashura, when the tents were burned and the survivors were left on open ground with nobody obliged to come for them.
Shahnameh [shaah-naa-MEH] — The Book of Kings. Ferdowsi’s epic, some fifty thousand lines, completed around the year 1000.
shoor [SHOOR] — Persian, fervour; also salty. The fast final section of a mourning night.
Siavash [see-yaa-VASH] — the innocent prince. Accused of a thing he did not do, proved by fire, exiled, killed in a foreign country over a basin.
Siavashgerd [see-yaa-vash-GERD] — the place Siavash made. The city he built in exile.
sofreh [sof-REH] — Persian, a cloth spread on the floor for eating.
Sudabeh [soo-daa-BEH] — wife of Kavus. She wanted Siavash, was refused, and accused him. She is not a monster in the poem — she is a woman in a palace with one kind of power.
Sug-e Siavash [SOOG-e see-yaa-VASH] — the Mourning of Siavash.
An annual rite of lamentation practised in Iran and Central Asia for centuries before Islam, and recorded by historians who complained about the noise.
Turan [too-RAAN] — the country beyond the river; Iran’s enemy in the
Shahnameh.
Zabolestan [zaa-bo-les-TAAN] — the eastern land of Rostam’s family.
